articles.title_orig: Clay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports bros, trans panic and mortgages
articles.title_zh: Clay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports bros, trans panic and mortgages
articles.content_orig:
The rightwing media mogul has lost ground to the likes of Pat McAfee and Joe Rogan. He’s hoping his new venture can recapture some ground
W hen Maga media blowhard Clay Travis offered $2m to Colin Kaepernick last week to appear on the daily talkshow he hosts with former CIA analyst Buck Sexton, it represented the culmination of a years-long obsession on the right with the onetime NFL star. In Travis’s telling of history, Kaepernick taking a knee during the 2016 NFL season was the event that catalyzed professional sports into the era of “woke” excess from which, he claims, it has been struggling to recover ever since.
But more than simply confirming the right’s longstanding villainization of Kaepernick, Travis’s offer was also a smarmy bid for publicity for his new media venture, Sport & State. Sport & State, which launched in August, is Travis’s bid to get back to his roots as a media mogul who sold the wildly popular Outkick to Fox Sports for a rumored $100m, and reclaim some of the cultural territory lost to fellow sports bros and Magagitators like Pat McAfee, Joe Rogan, Tucker Carlson and Ben Shapiro. But if there’s one thing Sport & State won’t be doing, it’s engaging with anyone beyond the Magaverse. There has been no response from Kaepernick since Travis made his “offer” of $2m to charity in exchange for an interview, which suggests he understands that it was extended more in a spirit of trolling buffoonery than sincerity. No one associated with the left or progressive politics ever appears on Travis’s shows, for the simple reason that they are designed purely for the right to talk to itself. (Some would say the same could be said of the left, although the disregard for dissenting perspectives in the Magasphere seems way more extreme.) More than it heralds a renewal of Travis’s career or an injection of fresh energy into the Trumpist mediasphere, Sport & State is a case study in the stagnation that has taken hold on the right as Donald Trump stares down the barrel of defeat in November’s midterm elections.
Having spent the better part of the past two months listening to the Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show (which runs from noon to 3pm ET every weekday) and the Clay Travis Show (3-4pm), I can say with confidence that there are, in essence, only 11 topics a given day’s programming on Sport & State will cover: college football gambling picks; Trumpworld figures who are friends with Travis and Sexton; the wonderful job that these figures are doing in power (sometimes mixed with the preceding theme: “Our friend Kash, who is truly our friend, Clay and I are both buddies with him, he’s a good man,” Sexton affirmed on a recent episode); the low levels of testosterone apparently common among white males who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 (“white dudes for Kamala” is perhaps the gravest slur on the Clay Travis Show); trans women in professional sport (I haven’t calculated this precisely but at a guess I’d say this accounts for 20% to 50% of the discussion on any show that Travis hosts, even as the number of actual trans women competing in professional American sports remains exactly zero and there are probably fewer than 10 trans athletes in total in college sports); crime in America’s cities (in recent weeks the fixation has been Lindsay Clancy , but it’s liable to switch at any moment to Iryna Zarutska, Luigi Mangione, Charlie Kirk, Iryna Zarutska , or whatever murder happens to have taken place on that particular day in New York City); the problem with women (in summary: they are women); the fact that Travis and Sexton are both family men with wives and children; the fact that Travis has a law degree from Vanderbilt University; the fact that Travis studied law at Vanderbilt after he was rejected by Stanford (“I wanted to go to Stanford Law School, they didn’t want me, I went to Vanderbilt instead – I’ve now made a $10m donation to Vanderbilt Law School”); and the fact that Travis appeared on Fox News last night and will appear on Fox News again later today. Sprinkled throughout all of this are plugs for Hard Rock Bet (“Bet $5, get $100 in bonus bets”), which is the official gambling partner of Sport & State and holds equity in Travis’s upstart media concern, and companies such as Perfect 10 Mortgage, Crockett Coffee, XX-XY Athletics and Clay Travis Law, all of which – it should come as no surprise – Travis either outright owns or holds a stake in.
The recursiveness and self-referentiality of the advertising and content on Sport & State are all part of the site’s commercial strategy, according to Travis’s lengthy mission statement . The onshoring of all the advertising will, Travis claims, insulate his new venture from the vagaries of media’s traditional dependence on subscriptions and external advertisers. Gambling is the key revenue driver: Outkick became an affiliate of FanDuel after sports betting was legalized in 2018 and eventually made $350 for every new gambling account it helped set up, netting $2m in affiliate betting revenue on Super Bowl Sunday in 2021 alone, and Sport & State is set up to reap similar rewards through its partnership with Hard Rock Bet. But Travis’s expectation is that his home loan business, say, will also prosper as viewers stay online to hear his views on Ole Miss v LSU, Lane Kiffin or the apparent attempted hijacking of the Israel-bound passenger jet and what it means for the future of DEI in America.
Inadvertently, perhaps, Travis’s sidequest companies offer a sense of what Sport & State’s ideal audience member looks like: a patriotic American male with a habit of deploying the phrase “perfect 10” unironically whose life revolves around mortgages, coffee, litigation, gambling and moaning about trans women. On the Crockett Coffee blog , recent posts include “American Coffee Origins and Brewing Techniques”, “Discovering American Coffee’s Unique Flavors”, and “The Americano: A Complete History” (do I detect a theme here?); Travis sips throughout the day on Sport & State from a black spillproof coffee container, emphasizing his own commitment to the cause of caffeine and country.
If there’s a persistent “ Spider-Men pointing at each other ” quality to the advertising on Sport & State, that extends to the content as well. Travis’s big idea is that in the age of AI and commodified writing, it’s better to go deep than big, that depth of audience commitment matters more than the old traffic era’s scale-focused contest for clicks. There may be some wisdom in the strategy, but that approach – drumming down and appeasing an already loyal base – seems to have become the media-obsessed Trump White House’s guiding political strategy too, a choice that risks self-sabotage as the midterms loom. Travis’s theory of media is second-term Trump’s theory of power: instead of growing the audience, the electorate, the constituency, the sole purpose of having attention is to give those listening more of the same. Discussion on Sport & State this week included a summary of Travis and Sexton’s Monday meeting with Trump in the Oval Office. Their main point was to emphasize that “President Trump says he loves the show, says we’re doing a great job” and that various Trumpworld figures greeted them during their half-hour in front of the Resolute Desk. “We saw Karoline Leavitt, our very good friend”; “We also saw Susie Wiles – she said she is cancer-free now”; “We got a little quick high-five from Stephen Miller”.
Over a chyron announcing THE VOICE OF SEAN HANNITY, the longtime Fox News host then called in to discuss: sports betting (what else?); the border collie he’s about to take delivery of at the conclusion of nine months of dog training (if this is what it takes to survive domestic cohabitation with Hannity as an animal, imagine how things must be for the humans in his house); Gavin Newsom and Kathy Hochul as the highest-taxing, and therefore worst, governors in America; and potential Democratic candidates for 2028 (Hannity thinks AOC will be

articles.title_zh: France school protests: Hundreds of schools closed and 40 head teachers hurt
articles.content_orig:

Thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries, schools set on fire in France . When the summer vacation ended and the new term started just a month ago, few could have imagined that the academic year would so quickly descend into nationwide student protests — and turmoil.
In a country beset by crises — both foreign and domestic — the eruption and rapid spread of protests by unhappy teenage high schoolers caught France off guard.
Friday brought more of the scenes that have dominated streets this week: vandalism, garbage fires, teens confronting and taunting police. Officers charging, firing tear gas and making more arrests. By early afternoon, the education ministry reported protests impacting 560 schools.
Taking grievances to France’s streets has long been a rite of passage in the country that spawned the French Revolution of 1789. To name just a few, there were the student protests in 1968, weeks of suburban unrest in 2005 and demonstrations in 2023 against pension reforms.
The students now barricading high-school gates and demonstrating with placards have shown the know-how of veterans — down to wearing masks and googles against police tear gas.
The timing of these protests — with France engaged in a presidential election race — sets them apart. Candidates campaigning to succeed President Emmanuel Macron in May have seized on the demonstations as a hot political issue.
And although constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, Macron also joined the fray, speaking out against protest violence and political manipulation of the young demonstrators.
Here is what you need to know:
The demonstrations started in the Paris region
Protests first erupted last week in the Paris region and spread nationwide like wildfire, even to smaller towns.
High schoolers are expressing broad grievances — mainly, schools are under-resourced, with dilapidated facilities and insufficient staff. Still, spending on education is one of the costliest items in the state budget that Macron's government proposed this week, with 65.5 billion euros ($74 billion) set aside for schools in the next year. That's more than the proposed 63.4 billion euros for defense.
Students also complain that school days, which often start at 8 a.m., are too exhausting and the university entrance system too complex. Some university students also joined the protests this week.
Government says it's becoming rioting, not legitimate protests
Macron's government has repeatedly said that it respects the right to peaceful protest. But it also issued written orders for police to break up protests that block access to schools and to rapidly put a stop to violence and vandalism.
Riot police have liberally used tear gas, wielded their batons and made arrests to disperse crowds.
Police and school staff have been targeted with explosive fireworks and other injury-causing projectiles. The interior ministry says acid has been hurled in some cases, and that those intent on destruction and looting have grafted themselves onto the high schoolers' movement and behaved like “criminals and vandals,” instead of “young people legitimately voicing their demands.”
Police made more than 1,900 arrests on Thursday, when 305 officers were hurt, the ministry said.
The protests and confrontations continued Friday, and unrest also spread to neighboring Belgium where about a dozen schools closed in Liege, a day after violence in the city and six arrests there.
The protests come against a backdrop of broader school concerns
There have been broader concerns in France that the schooling system is losing ground to those in other countries and failing in its mission to enable children from disadvantaged backgrounds to move up the social ladder.
Performance gaps are growing between highly advantaged and highly disadvantaged students, and overall scores in reading comprehension and mathematics have plunged, according to the latest PISA report, which evaluates students worldwide.
The government banned smartphones from high schools when the school year started in September, with officials arguing that banishing screens will improve learning. France this year also became the first country in the European Union to ban social media platforms for children under 15, but the country’s top court struck down that measure.
The protests are impacting the presidential election campaign
The unrest is sharpening political battle lines between presidential candidates.
Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has positioned himself firmly on the side of the students and has decried police actions as “savagery” and repressive. Police have been suspected of firing firing crowd-control projectiles are suspected in some of the injuries that protesters have suffered.
Mélenchon's critics are accusing his France Unbowed party of stoking violence and seeking to score political points from the protests.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen has called for broader police powers against rioters. Conservative former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, one of Le Pen's main challengers for the presidency, has condemned those who “break things, burn things, or assault people.”
Associated Press writer Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Long-Term and Real-World Safety Data on Antipsychotic Agitation Therapy
articles.title_zh: Long-Term and Real-World Safety Data on Antipsychotic Agitation Therapy
articles.content_orig:
Longer follow-up and real-world claims data add context that pivotal trials alone cannot provide. The panel examines both, alongside how monitoring for response actually happens in daily practice.
"Long-Term and Real-World Safety Data on Antipsychotic Agitation Therapy" takes up the longer-term and real-world evidence behind an on-label antipsychotic therapy for agitation.
The panel reviews longer-term and real-world data on the antipsychotic option discussed in the prior episode. A six-month extension study, without a placebo arm, enrolled roughly 250 patients who had completed the earlier pivotal trial, focusing primarily on safety and durability rather than efficacy, and found no new safety signals. A separate real-world analysis, published in Neurology in 2025, used Medicare claims to compare new users of this on-label antipsychotic against new users of off-label aripiprazole, matching the two groups through propensity analysis and examining mortality, emergency department visits, and hospitalization. The on-label agent showed lower all-cause mortality than off-label aripiprazole, with no difference in hospitalization or emergency visit rates. The panel is careful to note this does not remove the drug's own black-box warning, but it is reassuring about real-world mortality risk relative to a commonly used off-label alternative.
The panel raises real methodological caveats, however, since aripiprazole's effects vary enormously across its dosing range, and the study does not specify dosing or comorbidities, such as coexisting schizophrenia, within the aripiprazole group, limiting how far the mortality comparison can be pushed. In long-term care, off-label aripiprazole for agitation is typically dosed at 2 to 5 milligrams, well below its psychiatric indications.
On monitoring in everyday practice, the panel is candid that formal CMAI and NPI scales, while valuable in research, feel impractical and exhausting for patients in routine care. Instead, clinicians track three to seven of the most troublesome caregiver-reported behaviors, prioritizing the most disruptive first, continuously reassessing safety, and checking at each visit whether prior concerns have resolved and new ones have emerged, while still inviting input from patients with only mild cognitive impairment when they are able to contribute.
Up next, in "What Drives Treatment Selection Between the Two On-Label Agitation Therapies," the panel weighs comorbidities and psychosis against long-term care rating pressures to choose between the two on-label options.

Nearly 85% of the assortment is available only at Target, including:

articles.title_zh: 'Tip Toe' Is a Harrowing Melodrama of Queerness and Masculinity in a World Gone Mad
articles.content_orig:

Tip Toe refuses to be misunderstood. Premiering Oct. 2 on Starz, the British miniseries from Queer as Folk creator and Doctor Who reviver Russell T Davies set its stakes as high as the lamppost from which Alan Cumming ’s character is seen hanging, dead, just outside his home, in the very first scene. Reminders of this awful outcome open each episode, preceding flashbacks that take us through the escalation of tensions between Cumming’s Leo Struthers and his next-door neighbor, Clive Goss (David Morrissey), over the course of just 10 days. Scripty speechifying and a finale that strains believability notwithstanding, Tip Toe is, in its unabashed melodrama, a harrowing cri de coeur about masculinity in crisis and queer liberation reversed.
Leo and Clive have a few things in common. Both pushing 60, the men have been sharing a wall in outwardly identical Manchester rowhouses for 14 years. They’ve also both, when we meet them, hit rough patches in life. Clive, an electrician, is having trouble finding enough work to support a family that includes touchy 16-year-old George (Jackson Connor) and 25-year-old Saul (Joseph Evans), who assists his dad on jobs but isn’t exactly earning the kind of money that would enable him to move out. As gossip swirls that he’s cheated on her, Clive’s wife, Marie (Pooky Quesnel), constantly berates him. Meanwhile, Leo’s longtime partner, Curtis (Charlie Condou), has left him for a woman. Not only is he unmoored in his personal life, overrelying on his indulgent best friend, Stephanie (Elizabeth Berrington); he’s also struggling to manage Spit & Polish, the bar in Manchester’s gay nightlife district that he and Curtis used to run together.
Alan Cumming in Tip Toe Starz
Early one morning, Leo chases after an anonymous hookup who has just absconded with his laptop—only to find himself locked out of his house in his underwear. Clive reluctantly lets him in to call Stephanie for a spare key, making clear all the while that Leo’s lifestyle disgusts him and that he’s uncomfortable having his neighbor around his sons, one underage and the other a musclebound Adonis. The thing is, Clive’s kids are nowhere near as innocent as he thinks. And he’s drawn further out of his comfort zone when Leo, against his better judgment, hires Clive and Saul to fix some wiring at Spit & Polish. The first sign of worlds perilously colliding is when a bar employee recognizes Saul from OnlyFans . An unsubtle but rhetorically effective montage of Leo and the Gosses, each in separate rooms, indulging in their preferred forms of pornography, reveals both the secrets they’re keeping from each other and the loneliness they share.
While Tip Toe spends time with all of these characters, Leo is its protagonist. And he’s an admirably imperfect one, charming and fundamentally kind but also pugnacious, prone to exaggeration, self-centered enough to earn Stephanie’s accusation that he doesn’t really value women. (She, in turn, shows glimpses of the J.K. Rowling-style transphobia that seems to afflict British feminists more than most.) His bar functions as a portal into the lives of less privileged members of the queer and trans communities, from his old, flamboyant, gender-nonconforming friend and unrequited admirer, Melba (Paul Rhys), to a 20-something trans bartender (Iz Hesketh), who’s calling herself Zee as she deliberates on a permanent female name—and who dodges transphobic violence daily. The question of whether the visibility Leo’s generation fought so hard to win has backfired, making them all easy targets, haunts the series.
David Morrissey in Tip Toe Starz
Davies recently raged against the homophobia of the early AIDS crisis in the searing period piece It’s a Sin and looked queasily ahead to a dystopian future in the sci-fi family drama Years & Years . Tip Toe unites their themes to complete a sort of trilogy, combining the anxieties of LGBTQ people, intrafamilial alienation, economic strife, the social-media panopticon, and an overarching sense of doom into a fire sermon against our toxic present. That it shares its Manchester setting with the far breezier, Y2K-era Queer as Folk underlines just how much that community’s outlook has changed in a quarter-century. And the fact that Cumming’s phenomenal performance is airing concurrently in the U.S. with The Traitors: New Blood , which he hosts with high-camp aplomb and an androgynous glam wardrobe, highlights the cognitive dissonance of a society where queerness is embraced—by everyone except the sizable faction that actively hates it. More than just Leo’s antagonist, Clive is an avatar for straight masculinity in crisis, desperately vulnerable but too terrified of showing emotion to say so. Morrissey captures that tightness of that bind. Devalued at home and work, he dabbles in conspiracy theories and marinates in videos of “real deaths.” His story can feel like an adult Adolescence .
Tip Toe also calls to mind other recent series ( BEEF , too many reality shows about feuding neighbors) and films ( Eddington , Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri ) that translate current political and social fault lines into tête-à-tête conflicts. On both sides of the Atlantic, storytellers are trying to understand the hateful tenor of the contemporary public sphere by distilling it down to its simplest, me-against-you form. The difference here is that, although Leo and other characters are shown to have healthy senses of humor, Tip Toe itself doesn’t share those titles’ tone of black-comic absurdity. It isn’t a funny show. Sometimes its seriousness veers into stridency. I didn’t find the abrupt escalation to Leo’s death particularly convincing.
Yet, as in It’s a Sin and Years & Years , it’s the incandescent clarity of Davies’ anger and fear that make Tip Toe powerful. For all the dumbed-down dialogue we get from streamers worried they’ll lose distracted viewers unless someone on screen recaps the plot every five minutes, it’s rare to hear characters plainly state things like: “History tells us one thing—that blood and fire and retribution always happen. And right now it’s coming for us.” When Stephanie confesses her worry that she’ll die in 30 years without living to see the pendulum of progress swing society out of what she calls a “new Dark Age,” I suspect she’s speaking for a lot of people. Too often in fiction (which this is, despite ending title cards that purport to update us on the characters’ lives post-Leo), social commentary is inoculated with optimism or couched in irony. In its unblinking earnestness, Tip Toe ’s melodrama accesses a truth that transcends any shortcomings of its plot.

articles.title_orig: New Preliminary Real-World VEOZAH™ (fezolinetant) Data Highlights Improvements in Menopause-Related Symptoms and Sleep Outcomes
articles.title_zh: New Preliminary Real-World VEOZAH™ (fezolinetant) Data Highlights Improvements in Menopause-Related Symptoms and Sleep Outcomes
articles.content_orig:
NORTHBROOK, Ill. , Oct 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Astellas Pharma U.S., Inc. (Head of US Commercial: Mike Petroutsas, "Astellas") presented a new preliminary analysis from the Phase 4 OPTION-VMS real-world study of non-hormonal therapies (non-HTs) for bothersome vasomotor symptoms (VMS, also known as hot flashes and night sweats) at the 2026 International Menopause Society (IMS) 20 th World Congress on Menopause. The analysis showed that VEOZAH (fezolinetant 45mg) treatment was associated with statistically significant improvements from baseline in bothersome VMS at week 12, the study's primary endpoint, and improvements were observed as early as week 4. 1 VEOZAH is approved in the U.S. for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.
Statistically significant improvements were also seen across patient-reported† and objective (obtained with a medical grade wearable) sleep measures for the first time at weeks 4, 8 and 12, including a mean reduction of 2.6 nighttime awakenings from baseline at week 12. 1
Sleep disturbances are among the most commonly reported and bothersome symptoms during menopause, affecting an estimated 40–60% of menopausal women. Women with moderate to severe hot flashes are almost three times more likely to report frequent nighttime awakenings compared with women without hot flashes. 2
OPTION-VMS is a Phase 4 real-world study of women prescribed non-hormonal therapies (fezolinetant, SSRIs/SNRIs* and other non-HTs e.g. gabapentin, oxybutynin) for bothersome VMS and other menopause-associated symptoms in routine clinical practice. 1 By combining women's reported sleep experiences with objective, wearable-derived actigraphy sleep data, OPTION-VMS provides new preliminary real-world insights into sleep outcomes in routine clinical practice. The study was not designed to assess differences between treatment groups.
The preliminary analysis found that women treated with fezolinetant experienced statistically significant improvements from baseline in:
No new safety signals were seen with fezolinetant. Hepatic laboratory findings were mild and infrequent (2 cases of non-serious mildly elevated liver tests), none of which led to treatment or study discontinuation. 1
Prof. Marla Shapiro, C.M., Department of Family and Community Medicine, University of Toronto, Canada, and lead author of the OPTION-VMS oral presentation , commented: "Hot flashes and night sweats can have a far-reaching impact on women's daily lives, including their sleep, quality of life and overall well-being. These preliminary real-world findings add to the growing body of evidence from OPTION-VMS, demonstrating improvements in bothersome vasomotor symptoms and sleep outcomes among women treated with fezolinetant. Taken together with the broader study findings, these data contribute to a more complete understanding of women's experiences in routine clinical practice and may help inform discussions between women and their healthcare providers."
These preliminary real-world findings reinforce data from the VEOZAH clinical trial program and are complemented by interim data from the ongoing GRACE real-world study in Germany and the ongoing ADELE-AU, real world study in Australia, also being presented at the International Menopause Society (IMS) 2026. 3,4
Additional data presented at IMS 2026 provide supporting pre-clinical, clinical and real-world evidence across different study settings and geographies. 5,6,7,8,9
Shayna Mancuso, D.O., FACOG, Executive Medical Director and Head, U.S. Medical Affairs, Women's Health, Astellas "These preliminary real-world findings provide valuable insights into outcomes observed with fezolinetant (VEOZAH), including sleep quality, among women experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes and night sweats. By evaluating women's experiences in routine clinical practice, we are building a deeper understanding of the outcomes that matter most to women and their clinicians."
Fezolinetant is a non-hormonal, selective neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist specifically designed to block neurokinin B binding on kisspeptin/neurokinin/dynorphin neurons, which are involved in regulating the brain's temperature control center. By targeting this pathway, fezolinetant helps reduce the frequency and severity of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause. 10,11 It is currently approved in 50 countries.
† Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Sleep Disturbance – Short Form 8b
* Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)/Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs)
About OPTION-VMS OPTION-VMS (NCT06049797) is a Phase IV, longitudinal, observational, study of women aged 40-75 years with confirmed menopausal hot flashes and night sweats (also known as vasomotor symptoms or VMS) who were prescribed a non-hormonal therapy for the treatment of bothersome hot flashes and nights sweats by their healthcare provider in a real-world setting. 1 The primary objective of the study was to check if the hot flashes and night sweats that bother women change after 12 weeks (3 months) of treatment from baseline; additional outcomes include sleep quality, menopause-related quality of life, sexual health, mood, work productivity and safety.
About ADELE ADELE is an ongoing real-world observational study of women in Australia over the age of 40 who are being treated with fezolinetant for moderate to severe hot flashes and night sweats, with sleep disturbances. 4 The primary objective of the study is to evaluate improvements in real-world sleep disturbances after 12 weeks of treatment. Additional objectives include better understanding of treatment satisfaction and adherence, and treatment impacts on menopause-related quality of life (QoL) and adverse events.
About GRACE GRACE (NCT07455812) is an ongoing 24-week real-world observational study of women in Germany who have menopausal hot flashes and night sweats and have been prescribed fezolinetant. 3 The primary goal of this study is to learn about the effectiveness and safety of fezolinetant through patient surveys conducted before participants' first dose, assessed through validated patient-reported measures, including symptom improvement, menopause-related quality of life, sleep disturbance, treatment satisfaction and safety, with follow-up surveys taking place 1 week, 12 weeks and 24 weeks after their first dose.
About VEOZAH TM (fezolinetant 45 mg) VEOZAH (fezolinetant 45 mg) is a selective neurokinin 3 receptor (NK3R) antagonist, currently approved in 50 countries for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause. Fezolinetant works by blocking neurokinin B (NKB) binding on the kisspeptin/neurokinin/dynorphin (KNDy) neuron, to modulate neuronal activity in the brain's temperature control center helping restore the balance in the brain's temperature control center (the hypothalamus) to reduce the number and intensity of hot flashes and night sweats due to menopause. 10,11
About Astellas Astellas is a global life sciences company committed to turning innovative science into VALUE for patients. We provide transformative therapies in disease areas that include oncology, ophthalmology, urology, immunology, and women's health. Through our research and development programs, we are pioneering new healthcare solutions for diseases with high unmet medical needs. Learn more at www.astellas.com .

articles.title_orig: The 1893 World's Fair Is the Subject of a New 'Chicago Stories' Documentary
articles.title_zh: The 1893 World's Fair Is the Subject of a New 'Chicago Stories' Documentary
articles.content_orig:
“This fair not only changed Chicago, it shaped the American imagination,” says Peter Marks, one of the producers and writers of the new documentary The World’s Fair of 1893 , which leads off a new season of our Chicago Stories on Friday, October 2 at 8:00 pm and at wttw.com/chicagostories . Walt Disney’s father was a carpenter who helped build the fair, while the illustrations of the Emerald City in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum, who attended, look “an awful lot like the White City” of the fair. The World’s Columbian Exposition not only inspired people; it also showed the world a new Chicago and introduced Vienna Beef, the zipper, and much more.
We spoke to Marks, his fellow producer and writer Tania Lindsay, and digital producer Meredith Francis about the fair, the documentary, and the companion website.
The Guide: Why is this World’s Fair so important to Chicago?
Peter Marks: This is the moment Chicago announced itself to the world. Only 20 years after the Great Fire , Chicago had transformed into an economic powerhouse and the birthplace of the skyscraper. [The skyscraper is the subject of another new Chicago Stories .] But people, especially New Yorkers, still dismissed us as a smelly ‘cow town.’ When Chicago beat out New York for the right to host the World’s Fair, Daniel Burnham and John Root had less than three years to turn a swamp in Jackson Park into a city that would dazzle and delight the world. Twenty-seven million visitors later, nobody could call Chicago a cow town anymore.
Tania Lindsay: It put the city on the map as a rival to New York and Paris. It also physically reshaped the city and seeded institutions, ideas, and products we still use daily.
The Guide: Why revisit the World’s Fair now?
Lindsay: Partly because there is no bad time to revisit the wonder that was the White City. And partly to remind Chicago of something about itself: That this is a city with a long history of doing hard and wonderful things, if imperfectly, and showing the world that we are much more than whatever the news says in any given year. The imperfect part matters too, and while we celebrate all the glorious wonders of the fair, the film doesn’t skip the hard parts, like who got left out, who got taken advantage of – or worse – and who carried on despite tragedy.
Marks: I think there’s something valuable about remembering a moment when Chicago took on the impossible. The fair is a reminder of Chicago’s “I Will” spirit, and what we can accomplish when we think big.
The Guide: How did you try to take a new approach towards a topic many Chicagoans already know?
Marks: One of the things we wanted to do was separate H.H. Holmes the murderer from H.H. Holmes the myth. Many people have read The Devil in the White City , in which Holmes builds this elaborate murder castle to lure unsuspecting victims. But that isn’t quite what happened. Newspaper reporters exaggerated the details, publishing fabricated diagrams of secret chambers and a crematory.
Meredith Francis: Another darker story to come out of the fair was the assassination of Chicago's mayor, Carter Harrison, just a couple days before the fair was set to close.
The Guide: What is something new that you learned in making this documentary?
Lindsay: Brownies can be highly controversial. While Bertha Palmer’s kitchen at the Palmer House Hotel is given credit as inventor of the beloved brownie, others question whether that apricot-glazed confection should be considered a brownie at all. It’s a highly sensitive topic. Some historians refused to comment, others cautiously avoided picking a side. Some said one thing off the record, and something different on. We may never know the right answer. But we’ll always have brownies.
The Guide: What’s something that most Chicagoans don’t know about the fair?
Marks: Most Chicagoans think the World’s Fair vanished, but it didn’t. If you walk down the Midway Plaisance at the University of Chicago, that’s where belly dancers once strutted and the first Ferris wheel spun. The Museum of Science and Industry was originally the Palace of Fine Arts. The Art Institute was created for the fair. There’s a ticket booth tucked in the yard of a private residence. The Obama Presidential Library rises on ground where the Horticulture and Women’s Building once stood. The fair is still very much around us if you know where to look.
Francis: On the companion website, we want people to be able to immerse themselves in this world, and to be able to imagine what it might have been like to attend the fair. We have some amazing historical images that go beyond the typical picture people might have in their heads. Our talented graphics team has created a really cool 3D imagining of what it would have been like to walk through the fair. It gives you a sense of just how expansive it was, and what it took to achieve that.
The Guide: What’s your favorite lasting impact of the fair?
Marks: For me, it’s Daniel Burnham’s vision. The White City helped inspire the City Beautiful movement and Burnham’s 1909 Plan of Chicago . There are times our skyline, parks, and museums still take my breath away.
Francis: There are a couple things that I would argue have made my life better: An early model of the modern dishwasher (invented by a woman!), and the brownie.
Lindsay: My favorite may well be the Ferris Wheel. I love that it exists because Chicago had a serious case of envy and wanted to top Paris’s 1889 World’s Fair stunner, the Eiffel Tower. George Ferris engineered the first-of-its-kind, giant wheel, with riding cars the size of city buses. It was a sensation when it debuted on the Midway Plaisance, which helped become the blueprint for the modern amusement park . Every time I see the wheel at Navy Pier, I see part of the Fair’s legacy, still spinning today.

articles.title_orig: Jobs Report Today: Bond Market Steadies as Investors Await Employment Data — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Jobs Report Today: Bond Market Steadies as Investors Await Employment Data — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures rose early Friday as traders assessed the release of September's jobs report.
S&P 500 futures were up 0.8%, while futures tied to Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 458 points, or 0.9%. Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 1.2%.
Treasury yields fell early Friday, with the 10-year yield dropping more than 5 basis points to 5.176%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
September's nonfarm payrolls report showed U.S. nonfarm payrolls increase by 29,000 in September, less than expected, with unemployment rising to 4.2%. The Dow Jones consensus called for job growth of 84,000 and for the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.1%.
The report comes as traders reassess the next move for the Federal Reserve. Fed funds futures trading suggests a 72% likelihood the central bank will stand pat in October.
Oil prices dropped sharply from their highs, following a report that European nation states are considering a release of strategic fuel reserves. The Trump administration has pressured European allies to "immediately" release supplies.
Front-month Brent crude oil futures were last seen nearly 3% lower at $99 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures were down by about 4% to $89 a barrel.
Investors are coming off a modestly higher session Thursday, to start off the month of October. However, all three indices are on pace for weekly losses, with the Dow off 1.7% in the period.
Those losses come amid a global bond market rout that has pressured stocks. On Thursday, yields climbed to multiyear highs before retreating sharply. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield soared to 5.344%, its highest level since 2002, then plunged to as low as 5.21%. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond also reached its highest in 24 years before tumbling as well.
Despite volatility in the markets, Luca Paolini, chief strategist at Pictet Asset Management, said he expects global stocks to "power on" thanks to strong earnings momentum.
"After a nine-month rally in equity markets and a recent spike in bond yields, stocks appear expensive relative to fixed income," he said in a Friday morning note. "However, we believe earnings growth remains a more powerful market driver. Companies in the MSCI World index are on track to deliver earnings growth of more than 30% this year, while emerging market firms could see profits rise by over 65%."
The U.S. economy added 29,000 jobs and the unemployment rate increased to 4.2 percent in September as job creation slowed substantially during the month, the Labor Department reported Friday.
Economists were expecting 84,000 new payrolls and the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.1%.
Here are some of the names moving premarket:
Click here to see more stocks making moves.
Shares for Seagate Technology and Western Digital slipped over 10% and 8% respectively after Toshiba announced plans to double its production capacity for hard disk drives used in data centers, according to a Nikkei report.
The Japanese company plans to invest $380 million to expand facilities in the Philippines, signaling Toshiba's first major hard disk drives investment in about five years, Nikkei reported.
Toshiba, along with Seagate Technology and Western Digital, are the top competitors in the hard disk drives market.
Morgan Stanley put Nvidia back atop its list of semiconductor stocks on Friday, touting the company's range of customers and the importance of graphics processing units (GPUs) to agentic artificial intelligence.
"While 90% of investor conversations are around the biggest hyperscalers and frontier model companies, half of the business - probably the faster growing half - is a broader range of AI model companies, Neoclouds, sovereign entities, ODMs and OEMs, and enterprise customers," Joseph Moore at Morgan Stanley wrote in a Friday note to clients.
Moore has an overweight rating on the stock with price target of $300 and an "industry view" listed as "attractive."
With its numerous backstopping and vendor agreements during the AI boom, Nvidia has faced criticism for being involved in circular financing during the AI buildout, which interlinks Nvidia's investments with its eventual revenue streams.
Oil prices fell more than 2% on Friday morning, extending losses from earlier in the session, following reports of a potential European move to release diesel and crude stocks to ease a global supply shortage
International benchmark Brent crude futures with December expiry traded 2.5% lower at $99.78 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with November expiry fell nearly 3.8% to $89.40.
It comes shortly after Reuters reported that European Union member states were discussing a French proposal to release additional diesel reserves following pressure from the Trump administration.
Moderna will replace Warner Bros. Discovery in the tech-heavy blue-chip Nasdaq 100 index after the biotech's shares have risen nearly sixfold over the past year.
The change will take effect before the market opens on Oct. 9, the stock exchange said in a statement late Thursday.
Shares of Moderna rose 2.4% in premarket trading, adding to a 563% gain over the past 12 months.
The company, which became a household name after it developed one of the first vaccines for Covid-19, surprised the Street last month when an experimental personalized cancer vaccine co-developed with Merck showed positive initial results in its first-ever late-stage trial.
Meanwhile, Warner Bros. is in the process of merging with Paramount Skydance . Paramount has said the merger will close on Oct. 6.
European government bond yields fell on Friday, as they headed for the end of a volatile week that saw yields on various regional securities hit multi-decade highs.
By 9:15 a.m. in London (4:15 a.m. ET), yields on British and German 10-year government bonds were around 7 basis points lower. Their Italian counterparts saw yields move 4 basis points lower, while 10-year bonds issued by France and Switzerland saw yields fall by 2 basis points.

articles.title_orig: Concerns About ‘WWII Allies’ at US-China Summit - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: Concerns About ‘WWII Allies’ at US-China Summit - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
At the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, both leaders spoke of the fact that the United States and China had been allies in World War II and had fought together. Of course, the United States and China (the Republic of China) were indeed Allied nations in WWII and fought together against Japan and others, and if the summit remarks were intended simply to reaffirm that historical fact and invoke shared memory, then they should give rise to no particular concern.
It is also worth recalling that in 2015, the 70th anniversary of the end of the war, U.S.-China relations were relatively stable, and China was emphasizing that it had fought alongside the United States and other major Western powers as key members of the Allied coalition, and had jointly created the postwar order. At that time, China was using the phrase “New Model of Major-Country Relations” in its relations with the United States. If the invocation of wartime partnership at the recent summit was intended to evoke memories of that 2015 period and signal an intention to restore the “New Model of Major-Country Relations,” that too would be comprehensible as a matter of Chinese policy.
However, more than ten years have now passed since 2015, and China’s narrative on history today is different from what it once was. So the fact that wartime partnership was raised by both sides at this summit is, in fact, a cause for concern. To explain, it is necessary to look at how China has recently been employing its historical narrative — with particular attention to its relationship with Russia.
The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 and China’s response to it, together with Russia’s war in Ukraine beginning in 2022, generated widespread international criticism of both countries. That criticism brought China and Russia closer together, and the two countries more openly positioned themselves in opposition to Western nations. In 2024, the 75th anniversary of the establishment of Sino-Russian diplomatic relations and a year in which the pandemic was still fresh in mind and the war in Ukraine was very much ongoing, Russian President Vladimir Putin made an official visit to China in May and issued a joint statement. It included the following passage:
“China and Russia will continue to firmly defend the results of the victory of the Second World War and the postwar world order enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations, and oppose the negation, distortion, and falsification of the history of World War II. They plan to solemnly celebrate the 80th anniversary of the victory of the Chinese People’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Soviet Union’s Patriotic War in 2025 and jointly promote a correct view of the history of World War II.”
This statement signaled that China and Russia intended to jointly insist on what they view as the “correct history” of WWII to the world, while refusing to accept any historical perspective that differs from their own.
In March 2025, at a press conference on the occasion of China’s National People’s Congress, State Councilor Wang Yi stated that, marking the 80th anniversary of victory in WWII, China and Russia were reaffirming that they had fought together in Asia and Europe at the cost of blood, and went on to say that, building on this past, the two countries would jointly promote a correct understanding of WWII history, defend the fruits of that victory, uphold the international system with the United Nations at its core, and advance the international order in a more just and reasonable direction. China and Russia have thus pledged not only to reaffirm their wartime partnership but to jointly seek to shape the present international order on that basis. For China and Russia, historical narrative is inseparable from the shaping of the current international order.
Then, on May 9, 2025, Russia’s Victory Day commemorating the defeat of Nazi Germany, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Russia and issued a joint statement with the Russian president. This statement explicitly identified Japanese militarism and Nazi Germany as the adversaries China and Russia fought in WWII, and made clear that China and Russia would together resist any moves to revive the militarism or Nazism of the past. On Japan specifically, the statement declared that “the Japanese government should learn lessons from the brutal crimes it committed in history, exercise caution in its words and deeds on historical issues such as the Yasukuni Shrine, and completely cut ties with militarism that once brought deep disasters to the peoples of the world and Japan itself.”
In its discourse on WWII, China was not only seeking to spread what it calls the “correct historical perspective” together with Russia, but was also issuing strong warnings against “Japanese militarism.” And this was positioned not merely as a matter of the past but — particularly in the context of the Sino-Russian relationship — as something linked to joint efforts toward a “just” reshaping of the international order.
In 2025, China made a qualitative leap in its narrative on history, in both substance and in method. China generated narratives connected to the invalidity of the San Francisco Peace Treaty, the Taiwan issue, and the status of Okinawa — areas directly linked to China’s interests in the First Island Chain. Yet China’s actions were moving faster than its words; its military activity had already extended well beyond the First Island Chain, expanding into the Second Island Chain, the Western Pacific, and the South Pacific.
From around the time of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s remarks in November 2025 and into 2026, China’s verbal attacks on Japan began to employ the term “neo-militarism,” and its criticism of Japan became more comprehensive. Japan’s security policy as a whole began to be characterized and challenged as “neo-militarism.”
In May 2026, when Putin made another official visit to China and a Sino-Russian joint statement was issued, language criticizing Japan’s “neo-militarism” and “remilitarization” was incorporated into the text, which represented an expansion of Sino-Russian historical cooperation on WWII. China also sought to extend its criticism of Japan to countries beyond Russia, inserting language critical of Japan — such as opposition to “militarism” — into joint statements issued in the context of bilateral relationships with various countries. At the UN General Assembly in September 2026 as well, the Chinese representative strongly criticized Japan using terms such as “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov joined in, expressing agreement with the Chinese position by similarly characterizing Japan as following a path of militarism.
Which brings us to the recent U.S.-China summit, where Xi and U.S. President Donald Trump raised the subject of the wartime relationship between the United States and China in WWII. The United States and China were Allied nations in WWII. But in light of the account above, China’s recent discourse on WWII is certainly not limited to pointing out historical facts or evoking memories of the past. And for Japan, that is cause for concern.

articles.title_orig: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
articles.title_zh: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
articles.content_orig:
Subscribe to our newsletter
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.
China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.
Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.
Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.
China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.
Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.
According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.
“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.
South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.
Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.
China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.
(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

articles.title_orig: Josh Jolly and Sienna Pal land on World Cup podium in China
articles.title_zh: Josh Jolly and Sienna Pal land on World Cup podium in China
articles.content_orig:
Home → ← News → Josh Jolly and Sienna Pal land on World Cup podium in China
The ARA Australian Cycling Team has finished Round 5 of the 2026 UCI BMX Racing World Cup with two bronze medals, won by Josh Jolly and Sienna Pal.
Jolly showed why his highly anticipated elite debut was worth the wait as he battled through the pack from a sixth place start to finish third in Mentougou, China.
The current under-23 world champion and former junior world champion slotted in seamlessly among the heavy hitters throughout the day after winning his first round moto.
A post shared by ARA Australian Cycling Team (@auscyclingteam)
The 20-year-old said reaching the podium in his first elite appearance was "awesome".
"I had high expectations of myself coming into the elite class and I’m happy that I proved to myself that I'm good enough and my expectations were correct," Jolly said.
"⁠I’ve been waiting for the day I move to elite on the World Cup series. I’ve just been trying not to make a big deal of it, so I don’t worry myself about being with the fastest guys in the world, and I've proved to myself that I'm one of the fastest in the world now too.
"In the final, I knew I had the speed around the track to pass anyone I needed too so I was confident in making moves."
Jolly's brilliant result was followed by a determined Pal scoring her second elite World Cup podium.
The 21-year-old dived down the inside of Switzerland's Zoé Claessens in the second corner and held the Olympic bronze medallist at bay down the third and fourth straights.
Only 0.036 seconds separated Pal and Claessens at the finish line, but it was enough for the Australian to clinch third behind Laura Smulders (Netherlands) and world champion Bethany Shriever (Great Britain).
A post shared by ARA Australian Cycling Team (@auscyclingteam)
"I feel so stoked. I was already happy and enjoying myself before finishing on the podium. This third is just a cherry on top and only good information to just keep doing what I’m doing," Pal said.
"In the final, I chose gate eight to just execute my process with less interruption. I felt most comfortable there so the plan was to execute and after that first jump just get to the inside as fast as I can.
"The last two years have been a bit of a rollercoaster since last being on the podium in 2024.
"Initially, I realised the potential but then started feeling the pressure. I’ve changed a lot with all my experiences since then, now knowing I belong here at the top level of this sport and keep that smile, follow your process and the good blessings will come when they come.
"Today was one of those good blessing days!"
Jesse Asmus narrowly missed the podium in his first outing sporting the world champion rainbow jersey, finishing fourth behind Jolly.
For Teya Rufus, a touch of wheels in the first corner of her quarterfinal that nearly brought the 20-year-old down ended her day despite a late charge back to fifth.
Round 6 of the UCI BMX Racing World Cup season will be raced tomorrow.

articles.title_orig: U.S., China buy more time to iron out trade wrinkles
articles.title_zh: U.S., China buy more time to iron out trade wrinkles
articles.content_orig:
When President Donald Trump recently hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping, there were expectations in farm country that some type of major deal would be announced to boost agricultural exports. Now, farm groups are analyzing the details and trying to figure out the timeline.
The White House released a list of goods due to receive reciprocal tariff reductions under a previously announced United States-China board of framework, which would affect $30 billion in goods from both the U.S. and another $30 billion from China. Potentially the deal could boost market access for U.S. farm products and improve access to the U.S. market for everything from Chinese toys and fishing tackle.
The deal essentially drops the country-specific levies on those products on the list, returning most to “most-favored-nation” status levels.
Dubbed the “30-for-30” framework, the announcement comes as the White House is seeking to forge stronger relations with Beijing after a tense trade war at the start of Trump’s second term.
“From agricultural products to medical devices, President Trump is unlocking improved market access for about 30% of U.S. exports to China, while benefiting consumers with imports from China of household goods, toys, and other products that the United States generally does not import from other countries,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a press release.
While the list includes U.S. wheat and corn, it notably did not include whole soybeans, which are still subject to a 10% tariff.
The American Soybean Association said it’s disappointed that soybeans were excluded from the list of products getting a lower tariff.
“China’s remaining 10% retaliatory duty limits access for private Chinese importers, meaning soybean trade will continue to be handled primarily by China’s state-owned enterprises. Removing the tariff would improve the competitiveness of U.S. soybeans and provide greater opportunity for private Chinese buyers,” ASA noted.
At the same time, ASA pointed to China’s continued commitment to purchase a minimum of 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans annually in years 2026, 2027 and 2028. These annual commitments provide important demand and greater certainty for U.S. soybean farmers.
“As soybean farmers look to strengthen and expand markets, China’s annual commitment to purchase 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans provides critical stability, and we expect those commitments to be fully met,” said ASA President and Ohio soybean farmer Scott Metzger. “China remains an important market for U.S. soybeans, and we want to see a strong trading relationship that allows more customers in China to purchase our soybeans.”
Soybeans weren’t completely left out of the agreement. The list identifies soybean seeds, soybean flour, soybean oil and its separated products, soybean cake and soybean residues, as in line for tariff cuts.
China is a big market for soybeans. The U.S. used to dominate the Chinese soybean market, but after the trade war during the first Trump administration, China turned to Brazil to fill that space.
Between October 2017 to March 2018, the U.S. exported 24.43 million metric tons of soybeans to China, according to USDA’s Economic Research Service . During that same time period in 2018-2019, Chinese imports of U.S. soybeans fell to 2.69 MMT. Brazil on the other hand, saw its market share grow by 11.47 MMT, increasing exports from 14.23 MMT. to 25.70 MMT.
The U.S. has struggled to regain that market. The Trump administration on Nov. 1, 2025, unveiled a deal in which China agreed to purchase at least 12 MMT of U.S. soybeans during the last two months of 2025 and at least 25 MMT of U.S. soybeans annually from 2026 through 2028. China has purchased roughly 12 MMT of soybeans since October 2025.
The list of U.S. goods to enter China outlined 1,619 items, many of which are agricultural goods, including livestock like cattle, goats, pigs, turkey, and chicken. It also opens the market to U.S. ranchers seeking to sell beef and pork products, or other meat items. The list also names fruits and vegetables such as broccoli, sweet corn, potatoes, bananas, and citrus fruits.
The framework will also open the market for U.S. dairy. It outlines food products made from malt extract, grain flour and dairy products, in addition to items such as milk, yogurt and whey.
The U.S. Dairy Export Council described the two-month extension of the tariff truce as a “welcome step forward.”
“We are encouraged by the inclusion of U.S. dairy exports on the list of products to be considered for tariff reduction,” said Krysta Harden, president and CEO, U.S. Dairy Export Council. “USDEC urges the Board to swiftly deliver the full elimination of the retaliatory tariffs that still weigh on U.S. dairy so our suppliers can compete on a more level playing field.
The export council also cautioned the administration on port fees.
“As wider talks continue, it is essential that proposed port fees on Chinese ships are not passed along to U.S. agricultural exporters. Added freight costs would undercut the very gains the Board of Trade is meant to achieve,” Harden added.
The deputies to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Greer and Chinese Vice Premier of the State Council He Lifeng will monitor the bilateral trade of the products covered by the framework and can make adjustment proposals; however, the two countries don’t imagine making adjustments more often than on an annual basis.
Editor’s note: Sara Wyant is publisher of Agri-Pulse Communications Inc., www.Agri-Pulse.com .

articles.title_orig: Broadcom Starts Amassing $60 Billion to Fund Chips for Anthropic
articles.title_zh: Broadcom Starts Amassing $60 Billion to Fund Chips for Anthropic
articles.content_orig:
Banks are set to syndicate a $42 billion senior-secured tranche, while Blackstone is leading an $18 billion junior debt tranche
Broadcom $AVGO is assembling $60 billion in debt financing to help Anthropic and other companies access AI chips and infrastructure, according to Bloomberg . For the deal, banks are readying syndication letters covering a $42 billion Class A senior-secured tranche, while Blackstone leads an $18 billion Class B junior debt tranche—putting up $9 billion of its own capital and planning to syndicate the rest, according to Bloomberg.
A representative for Broadcom declined to comment.
The deal has been in development for weeks and has drawn close attention from investors and dealmakers in both Wall Street and Silicon Valley, according to Bloomberg. The deal is seen as a gauge of continued appetite for funding AI infrastructure buildout at a time of public pushback against data-center construction.
The arrangement fits into a broader pattern of chip companies using their financial positions to drive hardware demand. Anthropic's IPO prospectus, which revealed the terms of Broadcom 's lending commitment to the AI company , showed that Broadcom has agreed to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion to help cover infrastructure spending. That amount would cover approximately one-third of the $125.2 billion Anthropic has committed under a five-year lease for tensor processing unit computing capacity, according to CNBC . The notes could be converted into Anthropic equity, and Broadcom has the option to bring in a financing partner under the terms of the deal, according to CNBC.
Anthropic is expected to become Broadcom 's largest compute customer in 2027, according to CNBC. Broadcom and Google $GOOGL have collaborated on multiple generations of TPU chips, and Anthropic announced in April an expanded agreement with Broadcom and Google for roughly 3.5 gigawatts of computing capacity built on Google 's TPUs, with that capacity expected to come online starting in 2027.
In its prospectus, Anthropic flagged that Broadcom 's dual position as a chip supplier and lender gives rise to "potential conflicts of interest" that could compromise Anthropic's access to the computing resources it needs, according to CNBC. The prospectus also noted that decisions Broadcom makes on pricing and equipment availability could undermine Anthropic's ability to build out its infrastructure, and that triggering certain payment or performance defaults could accelerate a material portion of its lease obligations while cutting off access to the $42 billion credit line.
The $60 billion package adds to hundreds of billions of dollars in debt already raised to build out AI infrastructure, according to Bloomberg.

articles.title_orig: What's really going on with the lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?
articles.title_zh: What's really going on with the lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?
articles.content_orig:
If she's ever feeling bloated, Abbey Alexandra has a go-to routine, using body oil and a wooden roller to perform stomach massages.
The 31-year-old from Birmingham shares before-and-after videos on TikTok, saying she feels the process leaves her depuffed and defined: "You definitely feel a lot better after, they are relaxing."
The technique is a form of lymphatic drainage massage, adapted from a medical treatment and shared as a beauty trend. Celebrity fans include Maya Jama, who shares her clinic sessions, and actress Hailey Bieber, who told Time magazine: "I swear by them."
Whether there is a physical change - or any need for one - is debatable, but fans of the massages claim they help "flatten" and "debloat" and give a "snatched waist" and "sculpted abs". But what's actually happening to their bodies?
Many videos on social media promoting lymphatic massage show a woman either standing sideways, facing the front or perhaps lying down with her stomach showing a slight - and very normal - curve outwards.
Then begins the methodical massage in circular motions seemingly draining fluid away. By the end, her stomach appears flatter - if a little red.
But social media body trends should always be viewed with scepticism, says Dr Ella Guest, senior research fellow and health psychologist at the Centre for Appearance Research based at the University of the West of England.
"These images might be altered using photo-editing tools or filters, people standing in particular poses, use of lighting, lots could even be AI-generated," she says.
"I think stopping to reflect on what you see and questioning whether it looks realistic, or if it's very aligned with beauty standards, can be useful. Remember, if something looks too good to be true, it probably is."
The lymphatic system is a network of channels and glands throughout the body that helps fight infection and remove excess fluid, according to the NHS.
Dr Xand van Tulleken tells Morning Live that the lymphatic system helps remove excess fluid from tissues and supports the immune system.
"When it is not working properly, it can contribute to swelling, which can be a condition called lymphoedema."
This commonly affects people who have cancers that involve the lymph system or who've had treatment involving the lymph nodes.
It causes swelling in any part of the body, but usually develops in the arms or legs.
"In simple terms, the lymphatic system helps keep your body's fluid levels balanced, cleans up waste, and supports your defences against illness," says van Tulleken.
Dr Xand says manual lymphatic drainage is one of a range of treatments used by medical professionals "if your lymphatic system isn't working as it should".
He describes it as using "light pressure" and "strategic massage techniques" to "clear" your lymphatic system.
"They'll coax excess lymph fluid from your swollen tissues toward your lymph nodes, where the lymph can reabsorb," he says - adding lymph nodes are found in the armpits, neck and groin.
He adds that these massages can be a "safe way" to relieve symptoms for conditions like lymphoedema but are not suitable for some people with pre-existing medical conditions.
He stresses: "No one should get their health advice from Instagram - far safer to use the NHS website, or consult your GP."
Abbey, who has endometriosis which she says causes her to feel bloated, began doing her own massage routines twice a week aer seeing social media posts about lymphatic drainage.
"I started using my hands and then I bought some wooden tools as well.
"After doing my routine, I personally feel less puffy and bloated, particularly around my stomach.
"Visually, I notice that my stomach looks a little more defined and I also feel lighter and more comfortable."
Dr Xand says there is "no need" for most people to perform lymphatic drainage treatments at home.
"There is very little high-quality evidence showing they provide meaningful or lasting benefits for healthy individuals, and it does not promote fat loss," he says.
But he does note that lymphatic drainage massages can feel "relaxing" and some people "can notice a temporary reduction in swelling".
"For most healthy people, regular movement, exercise and staying hydrated are all that's needed to support normal lymphatic function," he says.
"Unless someone has a diagnosed lymphatic condition, I don't think anyone needs routine lymphatic drainage treatments, despite the growing popularity of these practices on social media."
For Abbey, it's something she enjoys. "I know the visual difference is temporary... But I do like how I look and feel afterwards so it'll always be a part of my routine."
However, Guest warns striving for a sculpted stomach could "feed into people's insecurities".
"We know that when we compare ourselves online and try to live up to these trends, we tend to scrutinise our appearance more and feel less satisfied with how we look," she says.
"The reality is that healthy bodies come in a wide range of shapes and sizes."

articles.title_orig: Spanish protesters march on Parliament as emergency housing decrees are set to be rejected
articles.title_zh: Spanish protesters march on Parliament as emergency housing decrees are set to be rejected
articles.content_orig:
Spain's coalition government on Tuesday said it has agreed new measures to tackle the country's housing crisis after the forceful removal of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment in Madrid last week, sparked nationwide solidarity protests.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia said the housing legislation includes a ban on evictions until 2030, tighter rules for short-term rentals and a two-year extension for existing leases.
"It's ‌time ​to intervene in the speculative housing market and ​begin to rebalance the scales between ⁠citizens ​and vulture funds," ​Garcia, who belongs ​to the ‌leftist government's junior coalition partner Sumar, ​wrote ⁠in a post on ⁠X.
The Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his ministers, approved the measures after a meeting.
But since Sanchez leads a minority government, he is still dependent on votes from a number of other parties in parliament before the bill is set in law.
Sanchez's ruling Socialists were engaged in talks with coalition partners Sumar and others up to Tuesday.
Socialist Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez is scheduled to address a press conference later on Tuesday.
Images and videos last week that showed Maria del Carmen Abascal — known by her nickname Maricarmen — escorted out of her apartment by riot police officers touched a nerve among Spaniards who've long called for a solution to the housing crisis in the country.
Maricarmen's father had first rented the property in 1956 in Madrid's Retiro neighborhood and she continued as the tenant after her parents died.
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, after which a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.
According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company lasted eight years and their latest attempt to evict her from the apartment marked their fourth attempt to do so.
The issue placed Spain's housing market in the spotlight where many long-term tenants have been priced out of their apartments due to an affordability crisis and a shortage of homes in Europe's fourth-largest economy.
Protesters rallied around Maricarmen's cause, especially because pictures of her being taken out of her apartment building and into an ambulance were vividly present across social media.
She is a wheelchair user too.
People then hit the streets of Madrid in the thousands on Saturday, with many having ended their protest by setting up tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night.
More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.
Maricarmen's lawyer on Monday said that she was going to be able to return home, calling the victory a "result of the social mobilization."
"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters.
"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.
Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher
