articles.title_orig: Congo's Ebola outbreak has recorded over 4,000 deaths as authorities struggle to contain the virus - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Congo's Ebola outbreak has recorded over 4,000 deaths as authorities struggle to contain the virus - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths as authorities struggle to contain the virus
BUNIA, Congo -- Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases, making up for nearly half of the confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history .
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo’s ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons ranging from how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

articles.title_orig: Some of world’s strictest aviation security measures are under fresh scrutiny after in-flight attack
articles.title_zh: Some of world’s strictest aviation security measures are under fresh scrutiny after in-flight attack
articles.content_orig:
JERUSALEM — Israel has some of the world’s most stringent air travel security measures. The United Arab Emirates proudly adheres to international aviation safety standards. Yet those safeguards failed to prevent a flight between the countries from taking a dangerous plunge during an alleged attack in the cockpit .
The copilot allegedly stabbed the captain in the cockpit before passengers intervened aboard FlyDubai Flight FZ1073 after taking off from Dubai, UAE, with 182 people including eight crew members flying to Tel Aviv, Israel, on Wednesday.
The airplane made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday and the incident is under investigation by Saudi, Emirati and Israeli authorities, with the United States and Oman assisting efforts to determine a motive.
“Until this event, the possibility of a threat originating from a pilot or crew member was not considered a likely scenario. Security efforts have traditionally focused much more heavily on passengers and their luggage,” said Eyal Hulata, Israel’s former national security adviser. “That will probably change now and crew members will be subject to heavier screening.”
Israel’s security protocols focus heavily on Israeli airlines and departing flights from Ben-Gurion International Airport. A potential Achilles’ heel lies overseas, where procedures for Israel-bound flights vary and are harder for Israeli authorities to oversee.
Dubai International Airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal around a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.
“They are very conscious of the fact, a little bit like Israel in many respects, that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.
Pilot vetting and preflight screening aren’t uniform worldwide.
Investigators have not publicly identified the object used to stab the flight’s captain or said whether it was carried onto the plane or came from inside the aircraft.
Preflight screening of flight crews should generally “mirror very closely what a passenger goes through,” although security procedures vary around the world, said Dave Komendat, a senior security adviser at risk management firm International SOS and former chief security officer for Boeing.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
Israeli authorities have described the FlyDubai copilot as Omani. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations, raising questions about how the suspect ended up on the Tel Aviv-bound flight.
“Obviously, there was a loophole here. And we’re taking care of that,” Netanyahu said Thursday during an interview with Fox News Channel’s “Fox and Friends.”
Israel will increase security precautions on flights coming into the country whether or not they are operated by Israel. Pilots flying into Israel will be vetted and Israel will know their identities, prime minister’s office spokesperson Doron Spielman told The Associated Press.
There were no Israeli air marshals on the FlyDubai flight and the people who helped were civilians, Spielman added.
The International Civil Aviation Organization sets baseline pilot-vetting and licensing standards, while national regulators and airlines can impose additional requirements.
Aviation security expert Menachem Bachrach said Israel relies largely on foreign governments and airlines to vet their own crew members, and Wednesday’s incident may point to a compliance lapse rather than a flaw in the procedures.
“Before we’re jumping to tighten security, I would just say it’s likely that somebody didn’t follow the protocols,” Bachrach said.
Investigators to look for red flags and review distress call handling
Israeli flag carrier El Al periodically assesses its pilots’ fitness to fly, while other airlines may do so less often, said Arik Arad, chairman of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy CYVIATION and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion Airport.
Investigators will want to know whether colleagues previously reported concerns about the copilot and, if so, how the airline responded, Komendat said.
Investigators in the UAE and Israel also are likely to review responses to the distress signals that came from the FlyDubai plane after a steep drop in altitude.
A person who heard the FlyDubai flight’s air traffic control communications said a crew member reported a hijacking and requested ambulances. Authorities in Saudi Arabia and Jordan initially refused to clear the aircraft for landing, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
The crew member eventually persuaded Saudi authorities to allow the plane to set down at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in the city of Tabuk.
International aviation standards call for countries to give aircraft facing hijacking or other “unlawful interference” maximum assistance and priority. But the underlying 1944 treaty, the Convention on International Civil Aviation, only requires a country to provide assistance “as it may find practicable,” making it a “relatively soft obligation,” said Vincent Correia, co-director of McGill University’s Institute of Air and Space Law.
Standard practice in a serious emergency is to get an aircraft on the ground as quickly as possible at the nearest suitable runway, “regardless of nationality, flight plan or politics,” said John Gradek, who manages McGill’s Aviation Management Program.
Gradek stressed it’s still not clear why the FlyDubai plane took a 180-degree turn as it crossed into Jordanian airspace before heading southwest to Tabuk. It’s not unusual for flight crews to bypass the nearest airport in favor of one better-equipped to meet a plane’s needs, he said.
Locked cockpits have been central to flight security for 25 years
Netanyahu said the flight’s injured captain saved the aircraft and the 182 people on it by resisting the copilot’s attacks long enough to open the 737’s cockpit door, enabling passengers to subdue the suspect and other FlyDubai crew members to take the controls and land the plane.
Cockpit doors worldwide were reinforced and locked after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks to keep intruders out. The FlyDubai incident, and past crashes caused by pilots who wanted to take their own lives, highlight the risk when a threat comes from inside the cockpit.
“The industry itself needs to recognize that flight deck door — whilst installed for very understandable reasons to prevent a suicidal hijacking by a passenger — has also created a fortress into which the good guys cannot gain access to a rogue individual, be it a hijacker or a rogue crew member,” Baum said.
Airline personnel know more about aviation security weaknesses and can gain the trust of security workers they regularly encounter, Osprey Flight Solutions Chief Intelligence Officer Matthew Borie, whose company advises airlines on flight threats, said.
“Unfortunately, if an insider with nefarious intent wants to carry out something like this, they may actually be best placed to know where the most vulnerable points are and how to breach them,” Borie said.

articles.title_orig: Removing Red Tape Won’t Erase China’s Mining Advantage in Africa
articles.title_zh: Removing Red Tape Won’t Erase China’s Mining Advantage in Africa
articles.content_orig:
Recently, the top executive of KoBold Metals, a U.S. mineral exploration and development company, told Reuters that Western companies could catch up and compete effectively with Chinese companies in Africa if only red tape were removed .
I have to say, I was surprised by his confidence. Red tape is often blamed for the complexity and the lack of transparency of mining licensing and operations in Africa. Combined with the risks associated with many African mining jurisdictions, it can certainly deter Western capital.
Western companies would probably, as some might believe, be more competitive without the bureaucratic hurdles that slow them down. Chinese companies would welcome the removal of some of those hurdles too, even if they are less likely to say so publicly.
It’s not that Chinese companies are happy to deal with red tape, as some seem to believe. Speak with Chinese mining operators in Africa and you quickly understand how much they hate red tape; they deal with the same delays, uncertainty, and bureaucracy that frustrate their Western counterparts.
The difference is that many Chinese firms have nevertheless found ways to operate within these environments. How they do that is another question, and it’s not always one with comfortable answers. The lesson is not that Chinese companies have cracked some admirable code for dealing with red tape, but that they have managed to keep operating despite it.
Removing red tape would certainly help. It would reduce risk and bring more predictability to mining jurisdictions, which Chinese and Western companies alike would welcome. But I’m not so sure that alone would allow Western companies to catch up, as KoBold president Josh Goldman suggests.
Can Western companies match Chinese companies in their ability to raise and deploy capital, especially when Chinese companies can draw on state financing and other forms of government support? Can Western companies come with the whole package, offering infrastructure, financing, and commercial investment? Can Western companies match the political capital that Chinese companies have built over years in these countries — relationships that have helped some companies survive changes of administration and regime while maintaining their operations?
I have my opinions on how that competition would play out. We might even get a chance to see it in action, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where authorities are considering a one-stop shop to process billion-dollar mining projects regardless of investors’ origin. Politics and geopolitics aside, I’d be curious to see how Western companies would fare against their Chinese competitors under those conditions.
Then we might find out how much of the gap is really about red tape.
C. Geraud Neema is CGSP’s Africa Editor.

articles.title_orig: Lutheran identity in Norway and the United Kingdom
articles.title_zh: Lutheran identity in Norway and the United Kingdom
articles.content_orig:
Reflections on mission, identity and ecumenical relations were high on the agenda during a visit to London and Oxford by leaders of one of Norway’s northernmost dioceses.
Bishop Svein Valle (fourth from right) with deans from the diocese of Sør-Hålogaland in front of St Olav’s Norwegian church in London. Photo: LWF/P. Hitchen
(LWI) - A recent visit to St Olav’s Norwegian church in London felt a bit like a homecoming for Bishop Svein Valle, who leads the diocese of Sør-Hålogaland in northern Norway. Almost 30 years ago, he came to London with his wife and two young children to serve as chaplain to the congregation, which is also known as the Norwegian Church Abroad, or the Norwegian Seamen’s Mission.
“We were a bit adventurous and we wanted to experience something new,” he recalls, sitting in the sanctuary of the church, where the Norwegian government-in-exile regularly worshipped during the Second World War. Norway’s recently deceased King Harald was also a regular visitor and the church became a focal point for hundreds of his countrymen and women who gathered to attend memorial events following his death in August.
In the late 1990s, when Valle came to London (he began his ministry on the day that Princess Diana died), he says that many of his duties were still strongly connected with the support of maritime workers docking on the banks of the River Thames. “Norwegian ships were coming in all along the Thames, with sugar cane, or carbon dioxide to put in the beer, or oil tankers coming in from the North Sea. We visited all of them. We knew where the crews were from and we brought them newspapers from different regions of Norway,” he says.
How are we going to remain a church in 50 or 100 years?
Bishop Svein Valle, Church of Norway Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland
Three decades on, the bishop was back in Britain leading a delegation of deans from his diocese for a visit to London and Oxford, where they attended both traditional and contemporary worship services and held discussions on mission with their Anglican counterparts. “Our goal was to see what others are doing in the Church of England, where they have an ambitious plan to double the numbers of youth and children attending church by 2030,” he says, noting that declining membership is a challenge facing both Lutheran and Anglican churches.
The Church of Norway is a member of the Porvoo Communion of Lutheran and Anglican churches in Europe that have established full communion between and among themselves.
While the Church of Norway membership numbers around 60 percent of the population nationwide and 70 percent in his own diocese, Valle says he sees the trends elsewhere in Europe as “a warning sign.” Together with his deans, he has been reflecting on “how are we going to remain a church in 50 or 100 years? We know we need to do something today, so it was interesting to share ideas and to hear some Anglican perspectives.”
During his time as chaplain at St Olav’s church, he enjoyed close relations with Anglican and Catholic priests in his part of the city, located alongside one of the first tunnels for transport underneath the Thames. “We had monthly meetings with colleagues from the two Anglican churches, one a very low [charismatic] church and one a high [traditional] church, as well as with the priests from two Catholic parishes,” he remembers.
Bishop Svein Valle (right) with LWF Council member Dean Kristine Sandmæl in the sanctuary of St Olav’s Norwegian church in London. Photo: LWF/P. Hitchen
The visiting Church of Norway delegation deep in discussions inside St Olav’s Norwegian church in London. Photo: LWF/P. Hitchen
St Olav’s Norwegian church in London. Photo: LWF/P. Hitchen
“I feel that today we need to think more about so-called ‘mixed ecology’ church, which has different shapes and different people can find things to relate to,” he continues, reflecting on the outcome of 19 to 22 September visit. “What we do in Norway is fairly traditional, although we have choirs and youth clubs and some activities for toddlers too. But we can see that when children are attracted and regularly attend, they are socialized into the church and into the faith,” he says.
“There is a greater diversity within the Church of England, from very evangelical ways of worshipping to very traditional liturgy and music,” notes Dean Kristine Sandmæl , a member of The Lutheran World Federation (LWF) Council and a participant in the diocesan visit to Britain. “We know that our youth work needs refreshment, but how you do church in a big city with a university will always be very different from doing church in a small village with mostly older people,” she says. “The evangelical model is popular with young people, but it also comes with a more conservative theology and ethical perspectives and this is a big challenge,” she reflects.
Unlike the Anglican church in Britain, Lutherans in this country have always been a small minority, notes Sandmæl at the conclusion of the first in-person meeting of the bishop and all the deans in the diocese. “We have three new members of our team, so this has been an important time for all of us to reflect together,” she says. “Where we come from, people are just members of the majority church and don’t think so much about what it means to be Lutheran. I think this visit has challenged us to think more deeply about strengthening our Lutheran identity in our own context,” she concludes.

articles.title_orig: Powering China, reshaping Tibet
articles.title_zh: Powering China, reshaping Tibet
articles.content_orig:
To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Send a voice message to LivingPlanet
Subscribe to the podcast here via your favorite podcast app: Living Planet Podlink
Lobsang Yangtso: We would just lie down and then, you know, drink directly from the river with your mouth, and then I have this memory because when I turned over that side, you know, I could see a horse drinking at the same time as well. [laughs] Yeah, I mean, I remember that part. Yeah, I mean, you can just you know lie down … and drink directly from the river. You are making me to miss my homeland. [laughs]
For the first twenty years of her life, Lobsang Yangtso lives in eastern Tibet. Then she leaves. Twenty-five years pass before she comes home again.
Lobsang Yangtso: But now, you know, everything has changed.
The Tibet she returns is not the Tibet she remembers.
The no mads gone from the hills where she’d watched them grazing. Instead fences cut across the landscape. CCTV towers overlook villages. And the river from her childhood?
Nobody drinks there anymore, Lobsang says.
But what she's seeing in her hometown is part of something much bigger.
Around the world, countries are racing to cut carbon emissions - and demand is soaring for the resources needed to build a cleaner energy system.
No country is moving faster than China. It leads the world in building solar panels, wind farms, batteries and electric vehicles.
And much of what China needs is found on the Tibetan Plateau: rivers that feed some of Asia’s largest watersheds, along with copper, lithium and other critical minerals.
But this isn’t just a story about energy. It’s about land, culture and power - and who pays the price for progress.
Lobsang Yangtso: my homeland is one of the most beautiful places in Tibet. …
Today Lobsang Yangtso is an environmental researcher for International Tibet Network. As a kid, she ran through fields here, in high-altitude farmland surrounded by mountains. River gorges wind through the region. In the nineties, the mountainsides were dotted with slow-moving yaks, and semi-nomadic herders like Lobsang’s father.
Lobsang Yangtso: "...a few families would take all the yaks from all the households and then they go up on the mountain and then they come back. So it's based on the rotation, and they move from place to place. So it's like a very close way, supporting each other, living together and then especially during summer times, because of the high altitude, we get lots of you know the summer flowers...
Yellow poppies. Purple aster. White wild flowers that she can’t recall the name for.
Lobsang Yangtso: "...and people love to go for picnics, and it becomes community picnics. They love to keep horses in their houses as well. Tibet has lots of glaciers and streams and the small rivers are quite you know common."
In the summer, the river was still cool, fed by snowmelt from soaring mountain peaks. And in the winter, when it froze over...
Lobsang Yangtso: "...then ice skating was quite popular, even though we don't have a you know ice proper ice skating that we see, but … you would see small kids. You know, they have a small wooden chair or something like that, and then your friends pushing you, and then you’re just rowing. We have this belief of believing in the sacred mountain and sacred rivers, and because we believe in deities … we believe that if we exploit or extract any of the resources, or create pollution in that area, because of the deities, you know there is a possibility that you get harmed by that."
Lobsang left Tibet as a teenager. A monk from her village gave his blessing, and she was off to India for university. She didn’t know then that coming home would be so hard.
In the years that followed, the Chinese state imposed more and more restrictions on Tibet.
It took twenty-five years for Lobsang to get a visa to go home. Once she did, she wanted to lay eyes on the monastery she grew up worshipping in.
In the monastery, monks wore the same red robes. Police wore plain clothes.
Lobsang: "Even within the monastery, I could see a police station in the monastery."
Law enforcement had entered the monastery. What had vanished were images of the Dalai Lama, the Buddhist spiritual leader who fled to India in the 1950s, only a few years after Tibet was formally incorporated into the People’s Republic of China.
It was not only the monasteries that had changed. So had the land.
Lobsang: "When I was coming inside from Tendu to my hometown, another really strange thing that I have seen is that the sand mining that they do along the rivers."
Tibetan herders were reporting fish disappearing, and hundreds of yaks dying after drinking polluted water.  Locals said the pollution was a brew of toxic chemicals, leaking from mines upstream. The state is digging for what some call the white gold of the green transition – lithium.
Lobsang: "The river that used to flow in just in front of my house, people don't drink anymore."
Many of Asia’s largest rivers originate in the Tibetan Plateau – that’s why this region is called the "Water Tower of Asia." Downstream, an estimated two billion people rely on the flows that begin in this region.
But it’s not just freshwater that matters here. Today, the Tibetan Plateau is dotted with some of the highest saltwater lakes on Earth. And some of those lakes are reservoirs of liquid treasure: lithium, which we need for the batteries that are so crucial to the clean energy transition.
Meanwhile, locked into the rock of these mountains…
Copper and other materials mined here go into the solar panels that China produces so efficiently.
Some of the largest mines under Chinese state control are in Tibet, pumping out hundreds of thousands of tonnes of copper and other minerals each year.
But the mountains hold another prize for the clean energy transition … gravity.
Ruth Gamble: "The place with the most hydropower potential in Asia– well, actually the world, is the water falling off the sides of the east and the south of the Tibetan Plateau, so that's where the dams have been concentrated in the last-- since the since the end of the Three Gorges Dam in the last 25 years.
My name's Ruth Gamble. I'm the director of La Trobe Asia and a senior lecturer in environmental history at La Trobe University in Melbourne, Australia."
Dams work by storing water… and then letting it drop. The force of that fall turns turbines, and their spinning generates electricity.
Ruth Gamble: "What you have like on the edges of the Tibetan plateau where the water just pachooos down That's a technical term – pachooing [laughs] is where it just charges down off the side of the plateau – it’s the most potential energy, gross potential energy of any water on the planet because the descent is so steep, and the descent is so long, that it can it can create more turning turbines. It will turn more turbines than anywhere else on Earth."
All that falling water makes Tibet one of the most promising places on Earth for hydropower. But…
Ruth Gamble: "Everything else wants to slide down there as well. So landslides and avalanches and outburst floods are all going to come charging down that side of the slope as well."
The advocacy group International Campaign for Tibet counts more than 100 dams planned for Tibet that haven’t broken ground yet. They estimate these projects could displace more than a million people. But, they also estimate these dams would produce enough clean energy to electrify a country with the power footprint of Germany – so projects that could push a million people out of their homes could power tens of millions more with renewable energy.
Ruth Gamble: "It’s not just about whether you transition; it's about how you transition, right?"
China is still the world’s largest carbon emitter, and it’s still building coal plants at a cracking pace. Yet its clean energy buildout is also the fastest in the world, by a wide margin. To wrap our heads aro

articles.title_orig: Patient dies by suicide after "insurance issue" delayed medicine for lung disease flare-ups
articles.title_zh: Patient dies by suicide after "insurance issue" delayed medicine for lung disease flare-ups
articles.content_orig:
Kyle, Texas — Kenney Blewett was diagnosed with lung disease more than a decade ago but started experiencing flare-ups this year that made him feel like he couldn't breathe.
Blewett described those flare-ups as "the scariest thing in the world," said his wife, Cindy, adding that while the episodes typically lasted no more than a few minutes, they had become more frequent.
On top of that, simple tasks, like taking out the trash, left Blewett winded. He rarely left the house and had recently lost 45 pounds. "That sounds like cancer," Cindy remembered one of his doctors said. It was clear, she said, that her husband's poor health, tied to decades of smoking, was getting worse.
That's why, on June 2, Blewett's pulmonologist wrote him a prescription for a new medication to improve the terrifying breathing issues caused by chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD. But the prescription wasn't immediately filled. Two days after that doctor appointment, Blewett received an email from Walgreens explaining that, "due to an insurance issue that we're working to resolve," the medication was delayed.
"He was hopeful that it would work," Cindy said of the drug, two months after her husband's death. "I wish we had the chance to find out."
Insurance delays and denials have become an infamous feature of the American healthcare system, with nearly 7 in 10 adults calling them "a major problem," in a January KFF Health Tracking Poll .
In June 2025, six months after UnitedHealthcare's CEO was shot in New York, the Trump administration announced a highly publicized industry pledge , signed by dozens of major health insurers, to remove some of the barriers that block or delay patients from accessing doctor-recommended care. And yet that pledge was voluntary, and it carries no penalties if companies fail to comply. Indeed, a report published by KFF Health News in July found that some insurers that signed the pledge would not implement all the promised initiatives as originally outlined.
In recent years, lawmakers in most states, including Texas, have attempted to address delays and denials by regulating the insurance industry in the absence of substantial federal reform. But most health insurance plans, including traditional Medicare policies and employer-sponsored offerings, which together cover more than half of all Americans, typically aren't under state jurisdiction.
Even some medical office staff and pharmacy employees find the patchwork of state and federal insurance rules and regulations confusing, a problem that is poised to become more complicated as artificial intelligence plays a larger role in approving and processing claims.
"It's just gotten completely out of hand," said Matt Toresco, CEO of Archō, a patient advocacy and consulting company. He argued that patients need more assistance facing insurance hurdles.
The Blewetts' story illustrates how navigating these complexities remains a herculean task for patients and their caregivers.
Cindy has sought answers from Medicare, Kenney's private Part D drug plan, his pulmonologist's office, and Walgreens. She still has questions about who was responsible for the medication delay and how the holdup could have been prevented.
If the COPD flare-up Blewett experienced on the afternoon of Sunday, June 7, could have been avoided, she wondered, would he still have chosen to die by suicide that night?
During that first week of June, Cindy said her husband repeatedly asked if his prescription — a liquid medication meant to be inhaled through the nebulizer machine Kenney owned — was ready to be picked up from Walgreens.
Cindy said she wasn't initially surprised or worried by the delay. Since its acquisition by a private equity firm last year, Walgreens has cut thousands of jobs across the country, according to the Private Equity Stakeholder Project . Cindy said in August that their Walgreens pharmacy in Kyle seemed to her to have been understaffed for months, and that prescriptions were being filled more slowly.
When Cindy called the pharmacy a few days after Kenney's appointment to find out more about the insurance delay, she said, a Walgreens employee told her the prescription required prior authorization. Also called preapproval or precertification, prior authorization is a practice widely used by health insurers that requires medical providers to seek permission before their patients may receive covered treatment.
But Cindy didn't know which of Kenney's insurers required prior authorization for this medication.
For years, she had helped manage multiple policies on behalf of her husband. Kenney was insured by Medicare Parts A and B, the federal health insurance program for people 65 and older or with disabilities. But he also had a private Part D plan to cover drug costs through Wellcare Value Script, as well as a Medicare supplement plan through Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Texas — also called a "Medigap" plan — that paid for other out-of-pocket costs.
Initially, Cindy assumed that Kenney's Part D plan had invoked prior authorization for his new medication. But because it was a liquid that is inhaled through a nebulizer machine, this drug was one of relatively few covered by Medicare Part B's durable medical equipment benefit , not Part D.
The federal government had no record showing that this prescription had been billed to Kenney's Part B policy, the Medicare agency told Cindy over the phone, she said.
Sarah Tanner and Myriea Amaya, spokespeople for Centene, Wellcare Value Script's parent company, would not answer questions for this article.
After Kenney's death, when Blewett sought clarification at the Walgreens pharmacy, she said the employee "kept saying different things." She recalled his explaining that the prescription was submitted to Medicare Part B but without a necessary diagnostic code that the doctor should have included.
Carmen Lopez, a spokesperson for Walgreens, told KFF Health News in late-September that the company "cannot comment on matters involving specific individuals."
Subsequently, Cindy said, a district pharmacy supervisor for Walgreens reached out by phone, and told her the pharmacy tried to process the prescription through Part B on June 2, the same day as the pulmonologist appointment, but that the prescription was missing a diagnostic code from the physician. The supervisor said Walgreens sent a request for that code to the pulmonologist's office later that day, Cindy recalled.
Kenney's pulmonologist — Rajesh Shetty of LungDocs — did not respond to phone or email messages from KFF Health News. But Cindy said an employee at the practice told her they did not see a fax from Walgreens asking for a diagnostic code for the prescription.
Meanwhile, it couldn't have been an issue with Kenney's Medigap plan, since those policies don't require prior authorization.
"Short of getting attorneys involved," Cindy said, "I'm not sure how to find out what really happened."
Confusion surrounding these Part B and Part D distinctions is common, said Mike Hess, senior director of patient outreach and education at the nonprofit COPD Foundation. "Medicare has gotten to be so complex and convoluted over the years," he said, that even medical office staff and pharmacy employees often misunderstand the nuances.
And with the introduction of AI to the preapproval process, navigating insurance hurdles will likely get more complex for Medicare beneficiaries, doctors say.
Historically, traditional Medicare, unlike Medicare Advantage, used prior authorization sparingly. But in January, Medicare launched a pilot program in six states — Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, and Washington — testing the use of AI to preapprove some healthcare services.
It is intended to "root out waste in Original Medicare," CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz has said, but physicians and patients say the program is creating more red tape for Medicare beneficiaries and leading to inappropriate denials. The pilot program does not current

articles.title_orig: Mount Dora teacher uses social media wish list to feed hundreds of children
articles.title_zh: Mount Dora teacher uses social media wish list to feed hundreds of children
articles.content_orig:
Lisa Bell , Anchor/Reporter
Robert Breuer , Special Projects Producer
MOUNT DORA, Fla. – Meagan DeWitz may not wear a cape, but the Mount Dora teacher is making a powerful difference for children and families across Central Florida.
“I do this because there are so many children who go to bed hungry and wake up hungry,” DeWitz said.
DeWitz is a full-time third-grade teacher and a mother of two. While working at a Title I school, where most students come from low-income households, she saw that the school’s existing food program could not keep up with the demand.
“God put it on my heart,” she said.
So last August, DeWitz launched an organization called Squirrel Around the World. She began by sharing an Amazon wish list on social media, asking people to donate non-perishable food.
The response quickly grew beyond her expectations. Donations began arriving at her home from people across the country - and even from around the world.
“As soon as it comes in, it’s going out,” Dewitz said. “This is an everyday thing - even on the weekends, even on holidays, and even in the summertime, we’re feeding students and it never stops.”
In less than a year, Squirrel Around the World expanded from serving one school to helping 77 schools and organizations across Central Florida.
The need is often greatest for food that does not require refrigeration, a stove or even a kitchen. DeWitz says some families are experiencing homelessness or living in cars and hotels, making shelf-stable food especially important.
“All of our food is non-perishable,” she said. “It could be eaten right out of the package.”
The work can be overwhelming. DeWitz said she has cried in her driveway and carries stories of the families she helps that she does not always share publicly, but the support from what she calls her “squirrel family” keeps her going.
Sabrina Hutchinson, a third-grade teacher at Seminole Springs Elementary, said DeWitz’s work gives teachers peace of mind.
“Teachers, we tend to worry a lot about our kids when they go home,” Hutchinson said. “We know they’re going home and they’re getting dinner, and they are supported with that.”
Demand remains constant. DeWitz said there are times when the nonprofit’s shelves are nearly empty, but donations often arrive just when they are needed most.
“Last week was one of the slowest weeks of the whole year, and I was stressing out so bad because our shelves were empty,” she said. “Then, at the last minute, my squirrel family said, ‘Meagan, relax. We got this.’”
The shelves were soon filled again.
DeWitz hopes to eventually expand Squirrel Around the World beyond Central Florida and help children in communities around the world. For now, she said the nonprofit’s biggest need is not on her food wish list: warehouse space.
To learn more about Squirrel Around the World or find out how to help, visit the organization’s Facebook or TikTok page and Amazon wish list .

articles.title_orig: Trump’s ‘pitch perfect’ project announcements may be too late to help the GOP
articles.title_zh: Trump’s ‘pitch perfect’ project announcements may be too late to help the GOP
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is leaning into transactional politics in the final month of the 2026 midterm campaign , tying his administration directly to economic benefits in states that could determine control of Congress.
This week alone, Trump has promoted billions of dollars in proposed investments in Alaska and Iowa , redirected $20 million in Department of Homeland Security funding toward government-paid television advertising, and begun sending $500 checks to roughly 1 million people the administration says were overcharged for Affordable Care Act coverage under former President Joe Biden .
Trump is also taking the pitch on the road. The president traveled to Texas on Thursday to tour a Peterbilt Motors truck factory in Denton ahead of a campaign rally in neighboring Oklahoma. A White House official told Fox Business that Peterbilt’s parent company has seen a boom since Trump imposed tariffs on foreign trucks last November.
All of that comes on top of Trump’s promise last month that every American adult will get a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress.
The burst of activity amounts to an explicit effort to connect Trump and the Republican Party with material benefits for voters, just as early voting gets underway. It also comes as Trump has publicly acknowledged the White House is not doing a good job of promoting its accomplishments.
“We’ve done a great job and the thing I haven’t done a good job with is explaining it to people,” Trump told reporters at the White House before departing for Texas.
“I think the press isn’t covering us,” he said. “ We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don’t know about it because the press won’t talk about it.”
Pollster David Paleologos said transactional politics can motivate voters when they believe they are receiving something concrete, but can backfire when an announcement looks like an election-season promise rather than a lasting benefit.
“What usually happens is a political party tries to earn the trust,” Paleologos told the Washington Examiner . “If you don’t earn trust during that campaign year, then you resort to what’s happening now, which is an announcement timed right before early voting in earnest starts.”
Paleologos, who runs the Suffolk University Political Research Center, added that “transactional politics can be effective or it can boomerang if voters feel that this is a lame promise.”
The White House pushed back against the idea that Trump’s recent activity represents a late campaign pivot. Instead, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said that Trump started “carrying out an aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda on day one, which has been and will continue to deliver tangible wins for the American people.
“This president is delivering on his promise to stop Biden’s inflation crisis, drive economic growth, and create jobs, and there will be more to come in the next two years,” Rogers told the Washington Examiner .
Republican strategist John Feehery, a former aide to House Speaker Dennis Hastert, similarly argued that Trump should continue making the case through Election Day.
“This will be a close election and anything he can do to get his voters out will be positive,” Feehery said. “Every vote counts.”
But with Democrats holding an average 8-point advantage in generic congressional ballot polling, Paleologos said the question is whether voters believe they are actually “getting something” from Trump and Republicans.
BERNIE SANDERS LOOKS TO CEMENT POLITICAL LEGACY WITH 2026 MIDTERM WINS
“If voters are getting a check in the mail signed by Donald Trump, that has some immediate gratification and benefit,” Paleologos said.
“A promise is a promise. … But voters are also going to have to weigh that and say, ‘Is this the same promise that the president made about lowering gas prices or presiding over no wars as president and bringing peace to so many regions of the world? Is that the promise that we’re getting here or is this a real promise that speaks to the voters in these particular areas.’”

articles.title_orig: Pro-democracy activists increasingly vulnerable to authoritarian governments in Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Pro-democracy activists increasingly vulnerable to authoritarian governments in Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
A national flag of Thailand flutters in the wind with the city skyline in the background in Bangkok on September 9, 2026. AMAURY PAUL/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Last month, 26-year old Laotian activist Khieo Lapchanh disappeared on his way to his apartment in a Thai province just outside Bangkok. He didn't show up for his registration interview with the United Nations Refugee Agency in Bangkok the next day, and hasn't been heard from since, according to a human rights group tracking his case.
Days later, Australian democracy campaigner Tran Hiep, who was in Cambodia to meet with other activists of Vietnamese origin, similarly disappeared. Tran Hiep was due to meet his wife in Bangkok but never boarded his flight. This week, Vietnamese officials confirmed his arrest and that of the two other activists who were with him.
Tran Hiep, an Australian activist, was detained in Vietnam after a trip to Cambodia. He is photographed here by his wife, Chloe Dang, on a trip to Japan in May, 2026. Chloe Dang hide caption
"My husband entered Cambodia legally, and now he's gone missing and it appears [he's] in a Vietnamese prison somewhere," said Chloe Dang, Hiep's wife. "How can the Vietnamese government abduct someone on another country's land?"
Their cases underscore the precarious landscape for activists across Asia, who are increasingly vulnerable to transnational repression – hunted down by authoritarian governments even across international borders. Human rights groups have been warning of a "swap market" of repression in Southeast Asia, where governments in the region work together to intimidate, arrest, extradite and punish critics and refugees.
"Everyone has to be looking over their shoulder all the time," said Phil Robertson, director of Bangkok-based Asia Human Rights & Labour Advocates, who has tracked and advocated for victims of transnational repression for almost two decades.
In recent years, Cambodian opposition leaders say they have been surveilled and jailed in Thailand, once a refuge for asylum seekers. Laotian refugees in the country – verified and registered by the United Nations – have gone missing or been found dead .
Viet Tan, a pro-democracy group composed of members of the Vietnamese diaspora, published a report in September that documented 20 cases where Vietnamese authorities pursued critics and activists outside its own borders. These include blogger Duong Van Thai, who in April 2023 disappeared off the streets of Bangkok before showing up in detention in Vietnam. Thai, who was a U.N.-registered refugee seeking asylum, has since been sentenced to 12 years in prison.
"You'd expect there would be some larger outcry because what we're talking about is violation of refugee rights [and] of state sovereignty," said Robertson. But countries in the region have been "muted."
"It seems to almost be like: if you do something in my country… later I'll expect a favor from you," a trade where dissidents are mutually suppressed, he added.
Thailand's Ministry of Information and a spokesman for the Cambodian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Manushya Foundation, a human rights group that has previously assisted other Laotian asylum seekers, reported Khieo Lapchanh's disappearance to the Thai police.
The Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees, in a statement to NPR, said it does not comment on individual cases. It added that "states have the primary responsibility to provide protection and safety to persons on their territory, including refugees and asylum seekers and people whose lives could be at risk if they were returned."
Hiep, now 50, had moved to Australia more than three decades ago, said Dang, his wife. He lived in Melbourne, where he founded an advocacy organization focused on combating human trafficking of Vietnamese girls and women. The freelance IT professional was also passionate about free speech, Dang said, and helped those in the Vietnamese diaspora improve their digital security against the authoritarian state. They were texting about commonplace topics – issues with their fridge, preparing for Hiep's niece's birthday party – when he stopped replying on Sept. 18.
Viet Tan, the pro-democracy group, said Hiep was one of their members. So was Nguyen Duc Thuan, who disappeared from Cambodia along with Hiep on the same day. Thuan holds a Norwegian passport.
Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security said in a statement this week that it had arrested Hiep, Thuan and a third man, Thai Cong Truong Son, for trying to "cross illegally" from Cambodia into Vietnam. They've accused the three of terrorism and forging their identity documents. The Vietnamese government has designated Viet Tan as a "terrorist group," a charge the group denies.
Authorities have not specified where they are held and their families say they have been provided no information. The activists have not been granted consular access.
Dang has called for the Australian government to fight for Hiep's freedom, given he's a citizen of their country. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Vietnamese President To Lam met in Canberra last month, pledging to deepen their partnership on issues like defense and trade. Albanese, in comments to the media this week, said his government was providing consular assistance and engaging directly with the family.
"I'm not naive to say that I don't know [what the Vietnamese government can do]," Dang said. "But I hope as an Australian, his fate could be different."

articles.title_orig: Everything You Need To Know About The 2026-2027 ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Grand Prix
articles.title_zh: Everything You Need To Know About The 2026-2027 ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Grand Prix
articles.content_orig:
The 2026-2027 ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Grand Prix has officially arrived, and it is rapidly shaping up to be the greatest eight-man tournament the sport has ever assembled.
Featured in the incredibly stacked bracket are the undefeated and reigning ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Champion, a pair of Thai icons, hungry young lions, and a battle-tested Thai technician.
That bracket officially came to life over the past week, and on Monday, September 28, ONE Chairman and CEO Chatri Sityodtong took to Facebook to unveil the grueling road to the semifinals and grand final .
All four opening-round bouts are set across The Inner Circle 38 and The Inner Circle 39 , which will stream from Bangkok’s iconic Lumpinee Stadium exclusively for subscribers via live.onefc.com on November 13 and November 20, respectively.
Here is everything you need to know before the countdown begins.
The Inner Circle 38 kicks off the tournament with two quarterfinals carrying very different kinds of weight. Former divisional king Rodtang “The Iron Man” Jitmuangnon and ex-bantamweight ruler Nong-O Hama finally get the monumental matchup that was originally scheduled for ONE 173 in Tokyo, Japan, last November.
Rodtang’s granite chin and suffocating forward pressure have rarely been solved by anyone willing to stand and trade, while Nong-O counters with surgical timing and a missile of a right kick that has ended fights in an instant throughout his legendary career.
It is a clash of two contrasting styles and one shared refusal to ever take a backward step, with a combined 543 career victories standing between them heading into this quarterfinal.
On the same card , former WBC Muay Thai World Champion Shimon Yoshinari meets hard-hitting Lebanese firecracker Ramadan “The Scorpion” Ondash in a bout where legacy takes a back seat to raw ambition.
Shimon’s southpaw precision and body-hunting combinations have carried him to a perfect run under the ONE Championship banner, while the Lebanese warrior’s blistering speed and fearless aggression have made him one of the most explosive strikers on the global roster. Both men enter in career-best form, and neither has shown any inclination to play it safe.
The Inner Circle 39 raises the stakes considerably. Reigning ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Champion Asadula “The Dagestan Ninja” Imangazaliev runs it back against Aslamjon “El Pantera” Ortikov in a rematch of their instant classic at The Inner Circle 20 — a five-round war that had fans on their feet from bell to bell.
Imangazaliev’s suffocating pressure and finishing instincts collide once again with Ortikov’s technical, high-volume striking, with 26 pounds of gold and a World Grand Prix semifinal spot simultaneously on the line.
Rounding out the bracket, Black Panther and Ubaid “Bad” Hussain meet in a high-stakes collision between a battle-tested Thai talent and an undefeated British-Pakistani phenom.
The Thai’s grinding, opportunistic style has carried him through six straight wins, while Hussain’s balanced, ever-evolving arsenal has kept him perfect across 17 professional fights. Whoever survives earns a direct route into the sport’s biggest stage yet.
With the quarterfinals officially set, the shape of the final four is already coming into focus, even if the exact pairings remain a game of “what if” for now.
Should Rodtang and Shimon both advance, the tournament would pit generational power against generational speed — a potential five-round collision between one of the most durable chins in Muay Thai history and one of the sharpest young finishers in “the art of eight limbs” today.
Rodtang meeting Ondash instead would tell a very different story, pitting veteran composure against teenage fearlessness, with the Thai’s World Championship pedigree tested by an athlete who has never once shown hesitation against bigger names.
On the other hand, a Nong-O clash with either the Japanese or Lebanese youth would set up a striking clinic — the veteran’s technical precision matched against a level of speed and intensity he has rarely faced at this late stage of his career.
The other side of the bracket carries its own layer of intrigue, since there is no guarantee the flyweight Muay Thai king advances.
However, if the undefeated 13-0 Imangazaliev gets past Ortikov, a matchup with either Black Panther or Hussain would pit his supreme, unorthodox skill set — a puzzle nobody in the division has ever solved — against Thai grit or unrelenting freshness, depending on who emerges.
An entirely possible Ortikov upset, on the other hand, would send the newly minted number-one contender into a fight against two men who have never faced anything quite like his complete offensive arsenal.
Whichever pairing ultimately meets in the final, the 2026-2027 ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Grand Prix will certainly guarantee one thing: greatness will be earned, not given.
Every quarterfinal, semifinal, and final bout in this Grand Prix will be contested under ONE’s Global Muay Thai Rule Set , with standard non-title fights running three three-minute rounds.
There is one significant wrinkle, however. Unlike the ongoing ONE SAMURAI Featherweight Kickboxing Tournament and previous World Grand Prix tournaments on the global stage, this bracket features the reigning divisional king, Imangazaliev.
This means the ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Title will be on the line in every round of the tournament. As a result, those specific bouts with the gold at stake will be contested over the standard five three-minute rounds reserved for World Title fights in ONE.
Should the undefeated Russian fall short at any stage, the 26 pounds of gold changes hands independently of the bracket, and the standard five-round format applies for the remainder of his side of the tournament.
Either way, the math works out cleanly in the end: whoever wins the tournament final will be crowned the new ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Champion and the ONE Flyweight Muay Thai World Grand Prix Champion, claiming both the sport’s most prestigious individual title and its most prestigious tournament accolade on the exact same night.
All four quarterfinal matchups kick off across two action-packed cards, with Rodtang vs. Nong-O and Shimon vs. Ondash taking place at The Inner Circle 38 on November 13, followed by Imangazaliev vs. Ortikov and Black Panther vs. Hussain at The Inner Circle 39 on November 20.
Both events stream live in Asia primetime, exclusively for subscribers at The Inner Circle. Sign up today to make sure you do not miss a single second of the greatest eight-man tournament the sport has ever seen.
The dates and locations for the semifinals and the grand final will be revealed in the coming months.

articles.content_orig:
Years of decoupling showed that independence was an economically ruinous illusion while pragmatic bargaining yields vastly superior returns
Not so long ago, Washington’s approach to relations with Beijing was anchored by a single assertive phrase: dealing “from a position of strength”. It was rooted in a unipolar mindset: a belief that the United States could dictate terms, manage competition unilaterally and demand compliance from a distance.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI fires workers for mishandling 'sensitive information'
articles.title_zh: OpenAI fires workers for mishandling 'sensitive information'
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work which involved an external organisation analysing AI models.
"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.
The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.
The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity intensified in recent months.
"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," a spokesperson for OpenAI said.
Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.
OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites .
In an incident in July, one of the firm's AI models accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.
That incident led OpenAI to review the activities of its AI agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.
The firm said this week it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its systems.
Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, it said.
In September, researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic , called for AI development to slow down so its potential risks could be properly assessed.
Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman have also called for measures to address concerns over AI.
On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses - including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - to discuss AI.
After the gathering at the White House, Trump posted a document that he called a "morally binding" agreement that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.
Some technology experts criticised the pact, pointing out that it allowed AI companies to regulate themselves.
Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight of the technology.

articles.title_orig: ‘I couldn’t let everybody else die,’ says hero Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar
articles.title_zh: ‘I couldn’t let everybody else die,’ says hero Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar
articles.content_orig:
Smit Machchhar, the hero Flydubai captain who fought off a savage attack by his copilot , kept fighting because he could not “let everybody else die,” he said in his first public remarks since Wednesday’s suspected hijacking attempt.
“In that moment, I was fighting for my life,” Machchhar told India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was so severely wounded that I had fallen down… at that time, I was thinking what if I don’t get up?”
A horrific mid-air catastrophe on flight FZ 1073 heading to Tel Aviv was averted in a stunning turn of events on Wednesday when passengers bravely rushed into the cockpit and stand-in pilots regained control of the aircraft.
Machchhar was badly injured while trying to fend off the attacker. Images showed a gruesome scene onboard, with blood splashed across the cockpit and the seriously wounded pilot lying on the floor, his pained face partially covered with a mask.
Machchhar told Modi he was on the ground in the cockpit when he realized the plane was going down.
“And I knew in that moment – one last push, Smit! Just do it. The door is right there,” he said. “And even at that time, he was beating me up.”
“And then I just opened it… and then everybody came,” he said, referring to several other passengers who then rushed into the cockpit and restrained his attacker.
“I was doing this for my life, but at the same time, I knew that I couldn’t let everybody else die.”
Modi praised Machchhar’s heroics, telling the veteran pilot that his “courage, patience and quick thinking… saved the lives of so many people.”
“You yourself were fighting the battle of life and death,” Modi said.
Machchhar is recovering at a hospital in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE). He was initially treated for his injuries in Saudi Arabia, where the diverted plane was forced to make an emergency landing.
The father of two had suffered “massive blood loss” and was “severely wounded,” dentist Shota Musaev, a passenger on the flight who helped treat him, previously told CNN.
His bravery “managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told CNN on Wednesday.
Captain Smit Machchhar: The ‘jovial’ pilot and father who thwarted the Flydubai attacker
Machchhar appeared emotional in the call with Modi while recalling the ordeal, and apologized to the prime minister for crying on the phone.
The two later spoke in Gujarati, the language predominantly spoken by people from India’s western state of Gujarat, which is where Modi is from.
Machchhar said his daughter had come to visit him in hospital but got scared seeing him in his condition. His youngest son, who is two, has not been able to meet him yet, he said.
Born into a family in the textile business, becoming a pilot wasn’t Machchhar’s “childhood dream,” he told the Bona-Fide Banter podcast in 2025. Initially, he’d enrolled in a textile engineering course after school.
Speaking to Modi, Machchhar said he felt a sense of pride.
“Now that you have called me, I am really really proud of myself,” Machchhar said. “I wasn’t proud before this, but now I am.”
His wife, Sonal Machchhar, told CNN affiliate CNN News18 that the family had not asked him yet about what happened because “we don’t want him to get flashbacks of the incident.”
“We want him to fully recover, and I’m sure once he is in the right space to talk, he will share it with everyone of how the incident went on with him,” Sonal Machchhar said.
The plane’s co-pilot and Machchhar’s alleged attacker has now been transferred from Saudi Arabia, where the plane landed, to the UAE, where he faces a terrorism investigation.
A top UAE official on Friday described the mid-flight crisis as a “dangerous terrorist act.” Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic adviser to the UAE’s president, also cautioned against conspiracy theories as investigators look to establish the facts surrounding what happened.
The suspect is an Omani national, Netanyahu told CNN Thursday. Oman and Israel do not have formal diplomatic relations, and it is not yet clear how the Omani pilot would have obtained clearance to fly to Israel.
Authorities are yet to divulge the co-pilot’s identity. And there hasn’t been any confirmation of his motive or of the weapon he used in the violent altercation, though Netanyahu suggested to Fox News this might have been a knife or an axe.
The Israeli prime minister said the suspect had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination,” adding that it was too early to say whether he had connections to Iran or anyone else. He has so far stopped short of describing the incident as a terrorist act.
Netanyahu said the attacker was suicidal, adding that he had called out “kill me” after being restrained by other passengers.
US President Donald Trump suggested later Thursday the pilot may be linked to Iran , though he provided no details.
This story had been updated with additional details.

articles.title_orig: El Al forced to cancel first rescue flights to Dubai after authorities revoke landing permissions
articles.title_zh: El Al forced to cancel first rescue flights to Dubai after authorities revoke landing permissions
articles.content_orig:
El Al Israel Airlines has been forced to cancel its rescue flights to Dubai , the company announced on Friday morning, after Israeli airlines' permission to land there was revoked by the authorities.
El Al stated that, as soon as official permission is granted for the rescue flights to resume, it would be implementing the planned flights to bring stranded Israelis home.
Meanwhile, the Transportation Ministry said that "following coordination with all relevant parties, it was agreed that flights operated by Israeli airlines from Dubai to Israel would begin on Friday, October 2. However, due to the need to complete the necessary preparations and coordination by security officials for the operation of the flights, a delay is expected in the departure of the repatriation flights from Dubai.
“Citizens currently in Dubai should remain in contact with the airlines through which their tickets were booked and follow their instructions and updates,” the ministry added.
According to estimates, more than 10,000 Israelis are stranded in Dubai and at other destinations from which they had been expected to return to Israel via the United Arab Emirates .
Later on Friday, Israir announced that it had received the final approvals from the Emirati authorities and that flights would be departing from Israel to Dubai during the day. No similar announcement was made by El Al.
On Wednesday, a flydubai aircraft that departed Dubai for Tel Aviv was diverted and landed in Saudi Arabia following an altercation between the captain and the copilot.
During the incident, one of them was stabbed, prompting the activation of the distress signal.
The aircraft initially disappeared from flight tracking systems, raising concerns that it had been hijacked . However, after several tense moments, the circumstances surrounding the incident became clearer, and the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: How the fighting in Ethiopia spread beyond Tigray, in maps and charts
articles.title_zh: How the fighting in Ethiopia spread beyond Tigray, in maps and charts
articles.content_orig:
Fighting is intensifying across northern Ethiopia, almost four years after a peace deal ended a devastating two-year war in the country’s Tigray region.
The conflict has also spread into the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions. Government-aligned forces say they captured the strategic town of Alamata, Tigray, on September 28, while Tigrayan forces have pushed into Afar.
Telecommunications have been cut across much of Tigray and commercial flights have been suspended, separating families and hampering humanitarian operations.
Ethiopia’s army chief has accused Eritrea, Sudan’s army and Egypt of backing the armed groups, raising fears of a wider regional war. All countries have denied the allegations, with Egypt adding that it strictly respects the sovereignty of neighbouring states.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera maps where the fighting is, who is involved and how Ethiopia got here.
Fighting is concentrated in three regions in northern Ethiopia: Tigray, Amhara and Afar. There are several active fronts rather than a single battlefield.
In southern Tigray, government forces and their allies have taken Alamata, a strategic town about 120km (75 miles) south of the regional capital, Mekelle.
The town is a supply hub for troops, fuel and food near Tigray’s border with Amhara.
On September 22, between 15 and 17 drone strikes hit Alamata, including several schools and a hospital, according to the conflict monitor ACLED.
To the west, a separate front has opened near the Tekeze River in western Tigray, an area disputed between Tigray and Amhara.
Fighting has also spread into northern Amhara, around Kobo and Gidan in North Wello zone and Sekota in Wag Hemra zone, which government forces retook on September 27.
Further east, Tigrayan forces and the Afar armed group Ugugumo have advanced into Afar, where fighting has been reported along the Tigray-Afar border and around Erebti and Abala.
The advance matters because it could threaten the Semera-Djibouti corridor, Ethiopia’s main route for imports, including fuel.
Seven Ethiopian armed and political groups announced an alliance on September 20 aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establishing an inclusive transitional government.
The group is called the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, or the Alliance for Survival. Its members include:
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) : The alliance’s main military force, whose fighters launched the latest offensive. It dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018. War broke out between the TPLF and federal forces in November 2020.
The Amhara Fano National Movement: A coalition of Fano factions that turned against Abiy’s government in 2023, after fighting alongside federal forces during the Tigray war.
The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA): It has fought federal forces in Oromia since 2018, seeking greater self-determination for the Oromo.
The other groups named in the alliance are the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (also known as Ugugumo), the Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement and the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement. On September 25, the Sidama National Liberation Front announced that it would also join.
The alliance’s membership is contested. According to Jalale Getachew Birru, senior East Africa analyst at ACLED , the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement has denied joining, saying it has no armed wing. The ONLF is split: one faction backs the alliance, while another says it is not part of it. The OLA has indicated that its main interest is removing the government rather than joining coordinated military operations.
ACLED says only three members, the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and Ugugumo, were actively fighting federal forces as of September 26.
In its founding statement, the alliance accused the government of “dictatorial rule”. It said a transitional government would end the country’s wars, protect rights and open a national dialogue.
Ethiopia is a landlocked country in the Horn of Africa, bordered by Eritrea, Sudan, South Sudan, Kenya, Somalia and Djibouti. With about 139 million people, it is Africa’s second-most populous country after Nigeria.
It is also one of the world’s most ethnically diverse countries, with more than 80 groups. The Oromo are the largest, making up about 35 percent of the population, followed by the Amhara at about 24 percent. Other major groups include Somali (7 percent), Tigrayan (6 percent) and Sidama (4 percent).
Ethiopia is divided into 12 regional states and two chartered cities, Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa. The federal system, introduced in 1992 and formalised in the 1994 constitution, largely follows ethnic and linguistic divisions.
The renewed fighting stems from political and territorial tensions left unresolved following Ethiopia’s 2020-2022 Tigray war. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the federal government remain divided over political control, security and disputed territory.
Tensions have been building for months. According to the conflict monitor ACLED, clashes between Tigrayan and federal forces began near the Sudanese border on August 1, followed by federal drone strikes and Tigrayan troop deployments.
In September, Tigrayan forces moved tanks and artillery south. There were also reports of renewed recruitment and forced mobilisation in Tigray.
On September 20, the TPLF and six other armed and political groups announced the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, which aims to overthrow Abiy’s government and install a transitional administration.
Three days later, on September 23, fighting escalated sharply. Tigrayan forces seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire and pushed into neighbouring Afar and Amhara. The government says the TPLF launched an “all-out offensive”. The TPLF says it is fighting a “defensive war” and accuses federal forces of attacking with aircraft, drones and artillery.

articles.title_orig: DOJ charges Boston man with threatening conservative podcaster Katie Miller
articles.title_zh: DOJ charges Boston man with threatening conservative podcaster Katie Miller
articles.content_orig:
A Waltham man was arrested Thursday afternoon on allegations that he harassed Katie Miller, a conservative podcaster married to Stephen Miller, one of President Trump’s closest advisers, in a series of menacing, expletive-laced text and phone messages , according to US Attorney Leah B. Foley’s office and a social media post by Katie Miller.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, pleaded not guilty to a single charge of cyberstalking at an initial appearance and arraignment hearing in federal court in Boston, court records show.
Magistrate Judge Paul G. Levenson ordered Proia to surrender his crossbows, machetes, and passport, and to have no contact with the victim. He also restricted Proia’s travel to Massachusetts, and directed him to continue mental health services, and undergo random drug testing, according to court filings.
Federal prosecutors did not identify Katie Miller by name, instead describing the victim as a former political adviser and prominent figure in the Republican Party who lives in the vicinity of Washington D.C. and is married to a high-level federal government employee.
Stephen Miller is the White House’s deputy chief of staff for policy. Katie Miller is a former Trump administration official, where she served as an adviser and spokesperson for the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, until May 2025 and launched a conservative podcast that summer.
In a post on X, Katie Miller thanked federal law enforcement officials “for keeping me and my family safe.
“Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” she wrote.
A federal grand jury handed up Proia’s indictment on Thursday, court records show.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A message was sent to Proia’s attorney seeking comment.
Federal prosecutors allege that Proia made disturbing phone calls and sent text messages , more than 40 in all, from Aug. 3 to Sept. 23, to the victim and her parents.
In a call to the victim’s mother, the male caller greeted her by name and asked if she was disturbed that her daughter was married to “such evil,” charging documents said.
In a communication with the victim’s father, Proia allegedly said, according to charging documents, “hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you ... Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”
According to Foley’s office, Proia used “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to harass the victim with multiple daily and late-night calls.
The caller’s phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers via Voice Over Internet Protocol or VoIP. The applications allow a user to obfuscate their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, Foley’s office said.
“As alleged in the indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband, and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.
“Cyberstalking can inflict real fear and harm, and we take these allegations extremely seriously,” she said. “Those who use technology to harass, intimidate, or torment others should understand that attempts to anonymize their criminal conduct will not shield them from prosecution. We will find you, and we will hold you accountable.”
Ted E. Docks, the FBI’s special agent in charge of the Boston division, said in the same statement that Proia engaged “in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
“Terrorizing someone isn’t some sick game, it’s a crime, which is why the FBI and our partners take it so seriously as we work to protect and serve everyone in our communities,” Docks said.
Tonya Alanez can be reached at tonya.alanez@globe.com . Follow her @talanez .
